items.headline: A 16B model on 1 GB of RAM
items.deck: The smolmaxxing project runs 16-billion-parameter models on a TV box and a 2013 iPad - with custom 1-bit kernels, a vocabulary diet, and a trick that pages model 'experts' from flash like a books-on-demand library.
items.lead: smolmaxxing is an open-source project with one mission: run the biggest language model possible on the smallest hardware you own. Its patched version of llama.cpp runs a 16B-parameter mixture-of-experts model on a Xiaomi TV box with 1.9 GB of RAM at 5.1 tokens per second - and even on a 2013 iPad Air with 1 GB of RAM.
items.body: smolmaxxing is an open-source project with one mission: run the biggest language model possible on the smallest hardware you own. Its patched version of llama.cpp runs a 16B-parameter mixture-of-experts model on a Xiaomi TV box with 1.9 GB of RAM at 5.1 tokens per second - and even on a 2013 iPad Air with 1 GB of RAM. The scoreboard is absurd: the TV box (an Amlogic chip with about 1 GB of usable RAM, Android 14, no root) runs Qwen3.5-2B at 7.7 tokens/s as its everyday model, and the jailbroken iPad (an Apple A7 from 2013, about 700 MB usable) runs a 1-bit 1.7B model at 24-26 tokens/s. Four techniques do the heavy lifting. First, kernels built for each chip: a 1-bit lookup-table kernel, plus repacked 2-bit and ternary formats for the TV's Cortex-A55, and special versions for the iPad's A7, which lacks dot-product instructions. Second, a vocabulary diet: most of a small model's vocabulary is rarely used, so those output rows get dropped - and on the TV a 'headless' mode kills the launcher and Google services while a model runs. Third, the star move: mixture-of-experts models only use a few 'expert' sub-networks per token, so the popular experts stay in RAM while the rest are read from flash on demand, with the next layer's experts prefetched - that is how 8B and 16B models run on 1 GB. Fourth, dense models bigger than RAM get streamed from flash at full speed. The catches are honest: you need their patched llama.cpp (stock builds can't load the repacked models), the iPad must be jailbroken, and every number is measured on the device itself across a 160-experiment public lab notebook, failures included.
ptrs: The project: smolmaxxing (MIT license) - a patch on llama.cpp that runs the biggest LLM a device can truly handle; every number measured on the device itself.

Scoreboard: Xiaomi TV Box S (1.9 GB RAM, ~1 GB usable, Android 14, no root) runs Qwen3.5-2B at 7.7 tok/s daily and a 16B MoE model at 5.1 tok/s; a 2013 iPad Air (1 GB RAM, ~700 MB usable, jailbroken) runs a 1-bit 1.7B model at 24-26 tok/s and the same 16B at 2.6-4.5 tok/s.
Technique 1 - kernels per chip: a 1-bit lookup-table kernel plus repacked 2-bit and ternary formats, with special builds for chips lacking dot-product instructions.
Technique 2 - shrink the model's footprint: drop rarely-used vocabulary output rows; on the TV, 'headless' mode stops the launcher and Google services while the model runs.

Technique 3 - page experts from flash: MoE models use only a few experts per token, so hot experts live in RAM and cold ones stream from flash on demand, prefetched a layer ahead - the key to 16B on 1 GB.
Technique 4 - stream dense models bigger than RAM at the flash's full speed.
Catches: the repacked models need the patched llama.cpp (stock can't load them); the iPad path needs a jailbreak; the repo's EXPERIMENT.md logs all 160 experiments, failures included.
items.why: You keep thinking local AI needs a monster rig, bro - these folks ran a 16B model on a TV box. Your 16GB PC is a supercomputer by their standards, and the same tricks (quantized small models, llama.cpp) are exactly how you squeeze it. Legendary constraint-hacking.
items.example: The repo's own receipt: on the TV box, keeping only the popular experts in RAM and paging the rest from flash is what lets the 16B Ling-mini-2.0 model generate at 5.1 tokens/s in about 1 GB of usable memory - and the same box plays Qwen3.5-2B at 7.7 tok/s as the daily driver.

questions.q: How can a 16B model fit in 1 GB of RAM?
questions.a: It's a mixture-of-experts model: only a few expert sub-networks fire per token, so the popular experts stay in RAM and the rest are read from flash on demand, with the next layer's prefetched.

questions.q: What two tricks shrink a small model's RAM use further?
questions.a: Dropping rarely-used vocabulary output rows, and on the TV a 'headless' mode that stops the launcher and Google services while the model runs.

questions.q: Can you load these models in stock llama.cpp?
questions.a: No - the repacked 1-bit, 2-bit and ternary formats need the project's patched llama.cpp.

items.plain: Big AI models are like huge libraries that normally need a mansion. This project keeps only the most-used books in the house and sends a super-fast runner to the warehouse for the rest, right when each is needed. That's how a TV box with the memory of a budget phone can 'think' with a giant model.
items.image_alt: A tiny paper TV set and an old tablet, each with a giant brain-shaped cloud compressed into it by a paper press.
items.info_alt: Diagram: a small RAM box holding two glowing expert blocks; arrows stream more expert blocks from a large flash-storage box below, one arrow prefetches ahead.
items.info_caption: Hot experts stay in RAM - cold experts stream from flash on demand - the next layer's experts are prefetched before they're needed.

items.headline: 60-30-10: the color budget
items.deck: Designer Stefano Peschiera's rule: give 60% of your layout to a neutral main color, 30% to a contrasting secondary, and 10% to the loudest accent you own - reserved for the buttons that matter.
items.lead: The 60-30-10 rule budgets color like money: your main color covers 60% of the design, a secondary color takes 30%, and an accent gets just 10%. In the Dribbble design blog's guide, designer Stefano Peschiera shares the workflow he built around it - and why the smallest slice should be the most vibrant.
items.body: The 60-30-10 rule budgets color like money: your main color covers 60% of the design, a secondary color takes 30%, and an accent gets just 10%. In the Dribbble design blog's guide, designer Stefano Peschiera shares the workflow he built around it - and why the smallest slice should be the most vibrant. The roles are strict: the 60% main color should be a neutral that's easy on the eyes, the 30% secondary should contrast nicely with the main to create visual interest, and the 10% accent should be the most vibrant of the three, because its job is to emphasize critical items like call-to-action buttons. Distributing colors in these proportions visually organizes the design and adds balance. His palette-hunting trick: browse nature photos on Unsplash and extract three main colors that already match the ratio, taking the most vibrant as the accent - mother nature is the best designer to steal from. His process trick: wireframe in grayscale first - spacing and layout before color, with gray tones keeping the wireframe from looking dead - then apply the palette and iterate. And his favorite color-theory trick: stay away from pure grayscale and pure black, because pure grays barely exist in real life; always add a bit of saturation so colors feel natural and familiar.
ptrs: The budget: 60% main color, 30% secondary, 10% accent - the proportions visually organize and balance a design.
Casting: main = neutral, easy on the eyes; secondary = contrasts with the main for visual interest; accent = the most vibrant, saved for critical items like call-to-action buttons.
Palette hunting: extract three colors matching the ratio from nature photos (his source: Unsplash); the most vibrant becomes the accent.
Process: wireframe in grayscale first - spacing and layout before color - then apply the palette and iterate.
Bonus rule: avoid pure gray and pure black - they barely exist in real life; add a little saturation so colors feel natural.
items.why: Your reel covers and thumbnails need this, bro: pick a chill background (60), a supporting color (30), and let ONE loud color (10) scream 'tap here'. It's the difference between a designed post and a sticker explosion.
items.example: Peschiera's own workflow: pull three colors off a nature photo that already follows 60-30-10, wireframe the whole page in grays first, then pour the palette on - vibrant color lands only on the call-to-action, which is exactly why people click it.

questions.q: Which color gets only 10% - and why?
questions.a: The accent: it's the most vibrant of the three and its job is emphasizing critical items like call-to-action buttons, so a small dose keeps it loud.

questions.q: What kind of color should own the 60%?
questions.a: A neutral that's easy on the eyes - it covers most of the design, so it must never tire the viewer.

questions.q: Why design in grayscale first?
questions.a: It forces spacing and layout decisions before color, a constraint Peschiera calls productive - the palette is applied and iterated afterwards.

items.plain: Think of an outfit: mostly one calm color (your suit), a second color for support (your shirt), and one small loud piece (a bright tie). Websites work the same way - 60% calm, 30% support, 10% loud - and the loud 10% is where the 'buy' button lives.
items.image_caption: A 10x10 waffle of the color budget: 60 cells main (neutral) - 30 cells secondary - 10 cells accent (the loud one)
items.image_alt: A 10 by 10 waffle grid: sixty quiet cells, thirty contrasting cells, ten loud accent cells in one corner.

items.headline: Three lamps run Hollywood
items.deck: Key, fill, backlight - the three-point setup is so standard in narrative cinema it's virtually a rule. Learn what each lamp does, then break the ratio on purpose for comedy-bright or noir-dark moods.
items.lead: Three-point lighting is the default grammar of filming a person: a key light provides the main illumination, a fill light softens the shadows it creates, and a backlight separates the subject from the background. Film scholar Paul Ramaeker's explainer in The Conversation shows how this convention - and the ratio between its lamps - quietly writes the mood of everything from musicals to noir.
items.body: Three-point lighting is the default grammar of filming a person: a key light provides the main illumination, a fill light softens the shadows it creates, and a backlight separates the subject from the background. Film scholar Paul Ramaeker's explainer in The Conversation shows how this convention - and the ratio between its lamps - quietly writes the mood of everything from musicals to noir. The setup is so prevalent in narrative cinema that it's virtually a rule, often supplemented by a small eye-light to heighten an actor's expression; its most stylised form, glamour lighting, turned Marlene Dietrich into an icon in Josef von Sternberg's films. Then there's practical lighting: sources that seem to come from inside the story-world - a visible lamp, a window, the neon-soaked streets of Blade Runner - which cinematographers also use to pour colour into a scene with gels. The mood knob is the fill-to-key ratio. High-key lighting (lots of fill, low contrast, even brightness) dominated 1930s comedies and musicals; low-key lighting (little fill, hard light, deep defined shadows) belonged to horror and crime, and became the soul of film noir - mystery and moral darkness through concealment. A Cornell study found light levels in film have markedly declined since 1935: early arc lights were so brutal their ultraviolet radiation gave actors 'Klieg eyes', and as film stock and digital sensors grew more sensitive, sets could go darker - kinder to actors, richer for mood. Cinematographer James Wong Howe saw it coming in 1931: lighting had stopped meaning 'enough light to shoot' and become 'a visual, emotional foundation' for the film.
ptrs: The three points: key light = main illumination; fill light = fills in shadows on face and background; backlight = separates subject from the backdrop (less critical in colour).
The extras: an eye-light to heighten expressions; 'glamour lighting' (think Dietrich in von Sternberg's films) built for star iconography.
Practical lighting: light that seems to come from inside the scene - a lamp, a window, Blade Runner's neon - often with coloured gels bathing the frame.
The mood knob: high-key = high fill-to-key ratio, low contrast, even brightness (1930s comedies and musicals); low-key = low fill-to-key, hard light, deep shadows (horror, crime, film noir).
The trend: a Cornell study found film light levels have markedly declined since 1935 - sensitive stocks and sensors let sets go darker, sparing actors the UV-burn 'Klieg eyes' of early arc lights.
The mission statement (James Wong Howe, 1931): lighting went from 'enough light to permit photography' to 'a visual, emotional foundation'.
items.why: You shoot reels, bro, and this is the oldest cheat code in the game: one main lamp, one shadow-softener, one behind you. Nail that triangle and your bedroom looks like a studio; then starve the fill for instant drama.
items.example: Tonight's test: face a window (key), bounce a phone flashlight off a wall onto your shadow side (fill), and put a desk lamp behind your shoulder (backlight). Then switch the fill off - same face, same room, and it suddenly reads as a crime film. That's the fill-to-key ratio doing the storytelling.

questions.q: What does each of the three lights do?
questions.a: Key provides the main illumination, fill fills in the shadows on face and background, and backlight separates the subject from the backdrop.

questions.q: High-key vs low-key?
questions.a: The fill-to-key ratio: high-key means lots of fill - low-contrast, even brightness (comedies, musicals); low-key means little fill - hard light and deep shadows (horror, noir).

questions.q: What is practical lighting?
questions.a: Light that appears to come from sources inside the story-world - a visible lamp, a window, neon signs - often used with coloured gels to bathe a scene in colour.

items.plain: Imagine photographing a friend with one flashlight: half their face goes black. Add a second, weaker light on the dark side and the shadows soften. Put a third behind them and they pop off the background. Movies are lit exactly like that - and how strong light two is decides if it feels like a comedy or a horror film.
items.image_alt: A paper bust lit by three bold lamp beams from three sides, each beam a different flat colour.
items.info_alt: Diagram: a head silhouette in the center with three lamps around it - a big key lamp from one side, a softer fill from the other, a backlight behind - arrows showing each beam's target.
items.info_caption: Key lights the face - fill softens its shadows - backlight peels the subject off the background; the fill-to-key ratio sets the mood.

items.headline: Jensen Huang resigns from Nvidia
items.deck: Nvidia's co-founder and only-ever CEO resigned after admitting a romantic affair with an alleged Chinese spy, per TechCrunch; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and the stock slide has erased over $855 billion since Friday.
items.lead: Jensen Huang has resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia, the company he founded in 1993 and led for its entire life, after admitting to a romantic affair with an alleged Chinese spy that sparked a U.S. national security crisis, TechCrunch reports. CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO while keeping her CFO role, and Nvidia's board accepted the resignation Wednesday.
items.body: Jensen Huang has resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia, the company he founded in 1993 and led for its entire life, after admitting to a romantic affair with an alleged Chinese spy that sparked a U.S. national security crisis, TechCrunch reports. CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO while keeping her CFO role, and Nvidia's board accepted the resignation Wednesday. The market reaction was violent: shares fell nearly 12% in early Thursday trading, and since Friday the stock dropped as much as 19% - a market-cap loss of more than $855 billion. The scale of what he leaves behind is hard to overstate: shares that traded around $15 before ChatGPT rose over 1,450% to a $243 all-time high, with market cap up $5.5 trillion to a peak of $5.88 trillion in early October; revenue grew from $5.93 billion in Q3 2023 to $96.22 billion by the second quarter, and profits nearly 88x, from $680 million in October 2023 to $59.69 billion as of July 2026. The company also named Harvey C. Jones - on the board since 1993 - as its first-ever chair of the board, who will likely lead the search for a permanent CEO. The succession problem is real: Huang ran a famously flat org with around 60 direct reports and no heir apparent, owns about 3.5% of shares with no supervoting rights, and the board had the power to vote him out at any time. Ripple effects hit the AI ecosystem fast - CoreWeave fell about 9%, Nebius about 16%, IREN 6.6% - with Nvidia holding $99 billion of investments plus $25 billion in commitments, including $30 billion in OpenAI and $10 billion in Anthropic. Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday, giving the industry its first look at life after Huang. On Hacker News, the story pulled nearly 3,000 points - community reaction there ran from shock at the personal scandal to debate about Nvidia's future, which is discussion, not verified fact.
ptrs: What happened: Huang resigned as president and CEO days after admitting a romantic affair with an alleged Chinese spy; the board accepted Wednesday; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO and stays CFO (TechCrunch).
Market hit: shares -12% early Thursday; as much as -19% since Friday; over $855 billion of market cap erased.

His legacy in numbers: shares ~$15 pre-ChatGPT to a $243 all-time high (+1,450%); market cap +$5.5 trillion, peaking at $5.88 trillion in early October; revenue $5.93B (Q3 2023) to $96.22B (Q2); profits ~88x to $59.69B (July 2026).

Governance: Harvey C. Jones (board member since 1993) becomes Nvidia's first-ever board chair and will likely lead the CEO search; Huang had ~60 direct reports, no succession plan, ~3.5% of shares and no supervoting rights.
Ripples: CoreWeave -9%, Nebius -16%, IREN -6.6% on Thursday; Nvidia holds $99B of investments plus $25B in commitments (incl. $30B into OpenAI, $10B into Anthropic); earnings land Tuesday.
HN colour: the story sat near 3,000 points on Hacker News - commenters debated Nvidia's future, but that's community discussion, not verified fact.
items.why: The man who turned a gaming-card company into the engine of the AI boom - the reason your RTX 4050 exists, bro - just walked out mid-supercycle. Whoever steers Nvidia next shapes what you'll train on, rent, and buy for years.
items.example: Watch the dependency web: Nvidia bankrolls the very cloud companies that buy its chips ($99B invested, $25B committed), so when the CEO news hit, CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN all fell the same morning - one company's gossip became an industry stress test.

questions.q: Who is running Nvidia right now?
questions.a: CFO Colette Kress, as interim CEO while keeping her CFO role; Harvey C. Jones was named the company's first-ever board chair and will likely lead the search for a permanent CEO.

questions.q: Why did Huang resign?
questions.a: Days earlier he admitted to a romantic affair with an alleged Chinese spy, sparking a U.S. national security crisis, per TechCrunch's reporting; the board accepted his resignation Wednesday.

questions.q: How big was the market reaction?
questions.a: Shares fell nearly 12% early Thursday and as much as 19% since Friday - over $855 billion of market value gone; AI-infrastructure partners like CoreWeave (-9%) and Nebius (-16%) dropped too.

items.plain: The boss who built the company behind almost every AI chip quit after a personal scandal became a national-security problem. His finance chief is minding the store, and investors knocked off more value than most countries' economies - because the whole AI world rents its engines from this one company.

items.headline: GPU fingerprints in public weights
items.deck: Researchers say six frontier models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group carry numerical traces matching export-controlled NVIDIA Blackwell chips - found not from leaks, but from the models' own published weights.
items.lead: A forensic analysis by Will DePue at Unemployment Labs finds that six models released since April 2026 by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group contain numerical patterns matching NVIDIA's export-controlled Blackwell GPUs - while earlier models from the same companies match the older Hopper generation. The evidence comes entirely from the models' own published weights, not leaks or insiders.
items.body: A forensic analysis by Will DePue at Unemployment Labs finds that six models released since April 2026 by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group contain numerical patterns matching NVIDIA's export-controlled Blackwell GPUs - while earlier models from the same companies match the older Hopper generation. The evidence comes entirely from the models' own published weights, not leaks or insiders. The method is genuinely clever: the researchers recover traces of the models' initial values - the random starting point of training - and then search for the hardware configurations that reproduce them, the numerical equivalent of matching a bullet to a barrel. For two models, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3, they confirmed the match on physical Blackwell chips. The caveats are stated plainly: the fingerprint identifies how the weights were created and supports - without proving - that Blackwell also performed the training; a specially configured AMD setup, also export-restricted, is the only alternative identified, excluded for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and considered very unlikely for the other five. And the findings show access to advanced hardware but do not establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated. U.S. officials and press reports had already alleged DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips - without publishing technical evidence; this report is the first public technical case. On Hacker News, commenters debated whether init traces can really pin down hardware - healthy skepticism, worth reading as community discussion rather than settled science.
ptrs: The claim: six models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group (released since April 2026) carry numerical patterns matching export-controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs; earlier models from the same labs match older Hopper chips.
The method: recover traces of the models' initial values from published weights, then search for the hardware and initial configurations that reproduce them - no leaks, no insiders.
The receipts: for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3 the match was confirmed on physical Blackwell chips.

The caveats (stated by the authors): the fingerprint supports but doesn't prove Blackwell did the training; a specially configured AMD setup is the only alternative (excluded for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, very unlikely for the rest); location, access route and any export-control violation remain unestablished.
The context: U.S. officials had already alleged Blackwell use by DeepSeek and Moonshot without technical evidence - this is the first public technical case.
HN colour: commenters debated how reliable init-trace matching can be - community discussion, not settled science.
items.why: This is your field's CSI moment, bro: model weights quietly remember the hardware that made them, and someone proved it in public. If you ever doubted that training details leak into artifacts, six frontier models just got read like fingerprints.
items.example: The recipe, straight from the report: take a model's public weights, recover traces of its initial random values, then search hardware configurations until one reproduces those traces - for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3, they ran the same init on physical Blackwell chips and it matched.

questions.q: How can weights reveal what GPU made them?
questions.a: The researchers recover traces of the model's initial values from the published weights and search for the hardware configurations that reproduce those exact numerical patterns.

questions.q: Does the fingerprint prove the chips were in China or that export law was broken?
questions.a: No - the authors say it shows access to the hardware class; it does not establish where chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated.

questions.q: Which labs and how many models?
questions.a: Six models released since April 2026 from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group; earlier models from the same companies match the older Hopper generation.

items.plain: Every typewriter used to leave slightly different marks on paper, so detectives could tell which machine typed a letter. This research does the same with AI: the numbers inside a published model carry tiny marks of the exact chip family that started its training - and six big models show marks of chips that aren't supposed to be exported to China.
items.image_alt: A giant paper GPU chip pressing its patterned corner into a field of tiny numbers like a fingerprint stamp.
items.info_alt: Diagram: a published model file, an arrow to a magnifier revealing tiny initial values, an arrow to two GPU chip shapes - old and new - with a check mark landing on the new one.
items.info_caption: Published weights - recover the initial values - search hardware configs until one reproduces them: the match lands on Blackwell.

items.headline: He built the app the subscription wouldn't
items.deck: ZigZag is free, open-source embroidery software for Mac and Windows - SVG to stitches, visual editing, and a built-in MCP server so an AI agent can design alongside you. Born, per its Show HN post, when a $300 machine demanded a subscription.
items.lead: ZigZag is a free, open-source (Apache 2.0) embroidery studio for Mac and Windows: turn SVG artwork into machine embroidery, edit stitches visually, and export PES, DST, EXP, JEF or VP3 files for almost any machine - or send designs straight to a Brother Skitch over Bluetooth. Its Show HN post frames the origin: a $300 embroidery machine needed a subscription, so the author built their own app.
items.body: ZigZag is a free, open-source (Apache 2.0) embroidery studio for Mac and Windows: turn SVG artwork into machine embroidery, edit stitches visually, and export PES, DST, EXP, JEF or VP3 files for almost any machine - or send designs straight to a Brother Skitch over Bluetooth. Its Show HN post frames the origin: a $300 embroidery machine needed a subscription, so the author built their own app. The editor is built in Rust and behaves like a compact Illustrator: pen, shapes, path tools, image trace for turning PNG or JPEG logos into flat-color shapes with thread-palette snapping, lettering with arcs and paths, a stitch player, and a density map that warns where stitches pile up. The AI angle is real: the studio runs a local MCP server (127.0.0.1:7878, localhost-only, origin-checked) with tools like add_svg, trace_image, check_design, render_preview and export - and an Agent panel can run Claude Code or Codex in the background to build the design while you watch, limited to design tools only (no shell, no file edits). Setup on Windows is a zip download (Windows 10 1709+ or 11; click 'More info - Run anyway' past SmartScreen); Macs get a signed DMG (macOS 11+). There's a CLI too: zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.pes -o preview.png does the whole conversion headlessly. The repo checks itself against the competition: full parity tables against the free Ink/Stitch and the paid Wilcom Hatch, listing what ZigZag covers and what it doesn't yet (pre-digitized fonts, 3D foam, motif fills). Every writer is verified by reading files back with identical stitch positions, and it's tested on a real Brother Skitch.
ptrs: What it is: free, open-source (Apache 2.0) embroidery software for Mac and Windows - SVG in, stitches out, visual editing, exports PES/DST/EXP/JEF/VP3, sends to a Brother Skitch over Bluetooth.
The origin (per its Show HN post): a $300 embroidery machine needed a subscription, so the author built their own app - 300+ HN points of maker applause.
The AI part: a localhost MCP server (127.0.0.1:7878) with ~30 design tools; an Agent panel runs Claude Code or Codex on the live document - design tools only, no shell, no file edits.
Windows setup: unzip the release, run ZigZag.exe (SmartScreen: More info - Run anyway, it's unsigned); or use the CLI: zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.pes -o preview.png.
Honest tradeoffs: parity tables vs free Ink/Stitch and paid Wilcom Hatch admit what's missing - pre-digitized fonts, monogramming, multi-hooping, 3D foam, gradient fills.
Trust markers: writers verified by reading files back with identical stitch positions; tested on a real Brother Skitch (PP1).
items.why: This is the whole vibe, bro: someone got paywalled by their own hardware and shipped a free Rust replacement - WITH an MCP server so agents can design in it. Even if you never sew, download it tonight, convert one SVG, and watch the stitch player. That's how you learn what agents-in-apps should feel like.
items.example: Zero-cost drill: install the Windows zip, draw a 50 mm circle badge with your name on an arc, run check_design, then hit the stitch player to watch it sew virtually. Feeling spicy? Connect an agent: claude mcp add --transport http zigzag http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp and ask it to 'check this design and show me the preview' - the repo's own suggested prompt.

questions.q: Do I need an embroidery machine to try ZigZag?
questions.a: No - you can import or draw a design, check it, preview every stitch in the stitch player and export machine files; the machine only matters for the final sew-out.

questions.q: How do AI agents work inside it?
questions.a: The studio runs a localhost-only MCP server with design tools (add_svg, trace_image, check_design, render_preview, export...); an Agent panel can run Claude Code or Codex on the live document, restricted to design tools - no shell, no file edits.

questions.q: What does it replace and what's still missing?
questions.a: It covers the core feature sets of free Ink/Stitch and paid Wilcom Hatch (per its own parity tables), but not yet pre-digitized fonts, monogramming, multi-hooping, motif fills or 3D foam.

items.plain: Embroidery machines need special files that tell the needle where to go, and the software for that is expensive or locked behind subscriptions. ZigZag is a free app that turns any drawing into those needle instructions - and it even lets an AI helper do the drawing steps with you, safely inside the app.

items.info_alt: Diagram: an SVG drawing, an arrow to a hoop of stitch lines, an arrow to a machine file card, and a small agent gear connected to the middle step by a dotted line.
items.info_caption: SVG artwork - ZigZag plans the stitches - export PES/DST/JEF for the machine; an agent can drive every step over MCP.

items.headline: Teach the index what your users ask
items.deck: Apple's ICML 2026 paper replaces the 'nearest centroid' guess inside RAG search with tiny neural nets trained once, offline, on what your real queries look like - same recall up to 8x faster, or 99% recall scanning 11x fewer keys.
items.lead: Retrieval-augmented generation lives and dies by maximum inner product search: turn the question into a vector, find the database key that matches it best, and hand that document to the model. Apple's machine learning team shows the classic shortcut - cluster the keys, route each query to the nearest cluster centroid - can be beaten by small neural networks trained once, offline, on the distribution of queries a system actually receives.
items.body: Retrieval-augmented generation lives and dies by maximum inner product search: turn the question into a vector, find the database key that matches it best, and hand that document to the model. Apple's machine learning team shows the classic shortcut - cluster the keys, route each query to the nearest cluster centroid - can be beaten by small neural networks trained once, offline, on the distribution of queries a system actually receives. The standard speedup splits millions of keys into k clusters and compares a new query only to the k centroids, searching exhaustively inside the best cluster - a factor-k speedup with a real flaw: a key can sit far from its own centroid yet close to your query, and centroid routing skips that cluster entirely, missing the true best match. Apple's insight is that the function mapping a query to its best inner product is the support function of the key set - a convex function, which means it can be approximated by input convex neural networks, and its gradient at any query returns the best-matching key itself. Two specialized nets result. SupportNet learns one support function per cluster, so routing asks 'how good is the BEST key inside this cluster for this query?' instead of 'how close is the centroid?' KeyNet goes further: it maps a query straight to its best-matching key vector, acting as a query rewriter in front of a standard IVF index like FAISS - predict where the answer lives, then let the index look there. Both are trained by plain regression: sample queries from the real query distribution, compute ground truth once by exhaustive search, train, done - an upfront amortized cost for a fixed database, repaid on every query. On Natural Questions (about 2.6M passages in 128 clusters), the small SupportNet hits 95% routing recall 1.9x faster than centroid routing (1.74 ms vs 3.36 ms), and scanning just 5% of the database, learned routers recover the true partition up to 92.6% of the time versus 87.5% for the centroid baseline. KeyNet reaches 99% recall up to about 8x faster (0.23 ms vs 1.8 ms), needs roughly 11x fewer scanned keys for the same recall, and scanning just 0.001% of the database retrieves the true key up to 96.7% of the time versus 86% for the raw query. The paper is 'Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions', presented at ICML 2026.
ptrs: The job: MIPS - given a query vector, find the database key with the largest inner product; in RAG, that key's document gets prepended to your question.

The classic shortcut: split keys into k clusters, compare the query to k centroids, search exhaustively inside the winner - factor-k speedup, but centroid routing can skip the cluster holding the true best key (a key far from its centroid, near your query).
The unlock: query-to-best-score is the support function of the key set - convex, learnable by input convex neural networks, and its gradient hands you the best key itself.

Two nets: SupportNet learns each cluster's support function (routes by 'how good is the best key in there?'); KeyNet predicts the best-matching key vector directly and works as a query rewriter in front of a standard IVF/FAISS index.
How they're trained: regression on real queries - sample the query distribution, compute ground truth once by exhaustive search, train small nets, amortize the cost over every future query.

Why queries matter: in RAG, queries are short user questions while keys are long curated documents - they look nothing alike, and production systems have a stable query distribution worth learning from.

Receipts (Natural Questions, ~2.6M passages, 128 clusters): SupportNet-S hits 95% routing recall 1.9x faster than centroids (1.74 vs 3.36 ms); at 5% of the DB scanned, learned routing finds the true partition up to 92.6% vs 87.5%; KeyNet reaches 99% recall ~8x faster (0.23 vs 1.8 ms) with ~11x fewer keys scanned.
items.why: You will build a RAG thing sooner or later, bro - everyone does - and the default tutorial teaches centroid routing like it's the final word. This paper is the cheat code: your users ask the same KINDS of questions every day, so train a tiny net on that pattern once and let every future query cash the check.
items.example: The paper's own gallery: for the question 'Who wrote The Eye of the World?', a FAISS index fed the raw query pulls weaker top-3 hits, while the same index fed KeyNet's mapped query lands the right passages - because the net moved the query to where the answer lives before the search even started.

questions.q: What's wrong with routing queries by nearest centroid?
questions.a: A cluster can hold a key that sits far from its own centroid yet close to your query; centroid routing scores that cluster low and skips it, missing the true best match.

questions.q: What does SupportNet learn?
questions.a: Each cluster's support function - so routing can ask 'how good is the BEST key inside this cluster for this query?' instead of comparing the query to a single centroid.

questions.q: How is KeyNet used without rebuilding the search index?
questions.a: As a query rewriter in front of a standard IVF index like FAISS: the net predicts where the best match likely is in embedding space, and the unchanged index searches from there.

items.plain: Imagine a library with a million books, grouped into 128 sections. The fast way to find your book is guessing the right section by its signboard - but sometimes your book is shelved oddly and the signboard misleads you. Apple trained a small assistant who has watched thousands of readers and learned which section really holds what each kind of question wants, so you walk to the right shelf far more often.
items.image_alt: Paper shelves of clustered dots, one stray dot glowing near a query arrow that a centroid signpost points away from.
items.info_alt: Diagram: a query arrow meets a road fork; the centroid sign points to a big cluster, while a small learned net redirects it to the cluster holding the true matching key.
items.info_caption: Centroid routing asks 'nearest signpost'; the learned router asks 'which cluster holds your best key' - and skips the miss.

items.headline: Font sizes by ratio, not vibes
items.deck: A modular scale is a ladder of sizes built by multiplying one base number by one meaningful ratio - like 16px times the golden ratio - so every headline, margin and column in a layout is related by design, not by guesswork.
items.lead: A modular scale is a sequence of numbers that relate to one another in a meaningful way: pick a starting number and a ratio - say 10 and the golden ratio 1:1.618 - then multiply and divide to generate every size in your design. Tim Brown's classic A List Apart essay shows how basing a whole layout's measurements on such a scale produces a visual harmony that arbitrary, easily-divisible numbers never quite reach.
items.body: A modular scale is a sequence of numbers that relate to one another in a meaningful way: pick a starting number and a ratio - say 10 and the golden ratio 1:1.618 - then multiply and divide to generate every size in your design. Tim Brown's classic A List Apart essay shows how basing a whole layout's measurements on such a scale produces a visual harmony that arbitrary, easily-divisible numbers never quite reach. Typographer Robert Bringhurst put it memorably: a modular scale, like a musical scale, is a prearranged set of harmonious proportions. Building one is easy: 10 multiplied by 1.618 gives 16.18, then 26.18, then 42.36; dividing gives 6.18, 3.82, 2.36. You then choose numbers from the scale for type sizes, line height, line length, margins and column widths - nothing is eyeballed. The craft is in the inputs. Brown's advice: start with the body text, pick the size at which it looks crispest (his was 18px in Minion), and let that confident visual decision anchor the whole scale. Choose a ratio that means something to the content - he chose the golden mean because Renaissance page proportions were built on it, and his typeface drew on Renaissance ideals. For more options, a double-stranded scale adds a second 'important' number - his was a 190px headline - and interleaves two scales, filling each other's gaps. There's even a calculator at modularscale.com, and Brown leaves the scale URL as a comment in his CSS so anyone can study or rebuild his exact measurements.
ptrs: The recipe: one base number + one ratio; multiply and divide to generate every size - 10 at 1:1.618 gives 16.18, 26.18, 42.36 upward and 6.18, 3.82, 2.36 downward.
Where it applies: type sizes, line height, line length, margins, column widths - every measurement comes off the scale, none from thin air.
Bringhurst's framing: 'A modular scale, like a musical scale, is a prearranged set of harmonious proportions.'
Picking the base: start from the body-text size that looks crispest in your chosen face - a decision designers already make with confidence - and grow the scale from it.
Picking the ratio: make it meaningful to the content - Brown used the golden mean for a Renaissance-inspired text face; music, geometry and history all offer ratios.
Double-stranded scales: add a second 'important' number (his: a 190px headline) to interleave two scales and fill the gaps.
Tooling: modularscale.com generates the numbers; Brown documents his scale as a URL comment in the CSS so the system stays reproducible.
items.why: Your thumbnails and layouts have headline sizes chosen by vibes, bro - admit it. One base, one ratio, and suddenly your 12px caption, 19px body and 50px headline are all family. It's the difference between a playlist and shuffle.
items.example: Brown's own worked example: body text at 18px, ratio 1:1.618, a 190px headline as the second strand. His CSS pulls every margin, column width and type size from that one generated ladder - and he left the scale's URL in a CSS comment so you can open the calculator and see every step.

questions.q: What two ingredients make a modular scale?
questions.a: A starting number (like your body-text size) and a ratio (like 1:1.618); multiply and divide to generate every other size.

questions.q: Where do you use the scale's numbers?
questions.a: For type sizes, line height, line length, margins and column widths - any measurement in the layout.

questions.q: What is a double-stranded scale?
questions.a: Two scales interleaved - generated from two starting numbers or ratios - giving more size options that fill each other's gaps.

items.plain: Think of a musical scale: only certain notes sound right together. A modular scale does the same for sizes - start with your body text size, keep multiplying by one ratio like 1.618, and every heading and margin you pick from that ladder automatically harmonizes. No more '18 or 20? eh, 19'.

items.image_alt: Five cut-paper blocks in ascending widths, each 1.618 times the last, like a staircase.

items.headline: The smash cut: earn the quiet, then break it
items.deck: Hold a scene long enough to feel safe - then hard-cut to its violent opposite. No dissolve, no warning. Cat People invented the bus version in 1942; Oppenheimer let the flash arrive before the sound.
items.lead: A smash cut is an abrupt, high-contrast transition in image, sound, tone, scale, or time: the outgoing shot has earned a state - quiet, prayer, resolution - and the incoming shot contradicts it without any polite blend. It is the cut you reach for when contrast itself is the meaning.
items.body: A smash cut is an abrupt, high-contrast transition in image, sound, tone, scale, or time: the outgoing shot has earned a state - quiet, prayer, resolution - and the incoming shot contradicts it without any polite blend. It is the cut you reach for when contrast itself is the meaning. The mechanics are strict. First, hold side A long enough to establish tone, scale, or apparent closure - a smash from nowhere, with no earned quiet, is only loud. Then cut hard to side B with a large change on at least two axes: brightness, loudness, shot size, subject class - silence to noise, interior to blast, hymn to murder. No dissolve, no fade; and you can coordinate picture and sound to smash together, or delay the sound for a second hit - the blast seen, then heard, which is exactly how Oppenheimer plays the Trinity explosion. The canon is full of it: Cat People (1942) lets a night walk tighten with dread until a bus hisses into frame - the scare was a vehicle, the cut both the joke and the slap; Carrie (1976) lets the grave visit settle before a hand breaks the earth; Whiplash smashes quiet into the drum kit; The Exorcist III stretches a hospital corridor into prolonged observation before a sudden attack. Know the cousins, because they get confused: a jump cut stays inside a similar frame and skips time; a flash cut steals a few frames of another image; a match cut rhymes two images; cross-cutting alternates two lines of action. The smash cut refuses the rhyme entirely. The common failure is sides that are too similar - same brightness, same scale, same tone - because then nothing smashes.
ptrs: Definition: an abrupt, high-contrast join in image, sound, tone, scale or time - one side has earned a state, the other breaks it without a blend.
Rule one: earn the first state - hold A long enough to establish quiet, prayer or resolution. A smash from nowhere is only loud.
Rule two: change at least two axes on B (brightness, loudness, shot size, subject class) - silence to noise, interior to blast.
Rule three: no dissolve, no fade - and sound can smash with the picture or arrive delayed for a second hit (Oppenheimer: the Trinity flash before the blast sound).
Canon: Cat People (1942, the bus that interrupts a tense walk), Carrie (1976, the grave visit that settles first), Whiplash (quiet into the kit), The Exorcist III (the long corridor).
Not to be confused: a jump cut skips time inside a similar framing; a flash cut steals frames; a match cut rhymes; cross-cutting alternates. The smash cut is contrast after an earned state.
The failure mode: sides too similar in brightness, scale and tone - nothing smashes.
items.why: Your reels live and die on the first second, bro - this is the atomic version of the hook. Earn one calm beat, then detonate the opposite. Cat People did it with a bus in 1942 and editors are still stealing the move.
items.example: Film 5 seconds of a dark, silent corridor - hold it until it feels safe. Then hard-cut to a bright, loud kitchen, mixer at full speed. That jolt is the whole lesson; and if you let the kitchen appear one beat before its sound arrives, you just did the Oppenheimer version.

questions.q: What must exist before a smash cut can work?
questions.a: An earned state on side A - quiet, prayer, or apparent resolution held long enough to register. Without it, the cut is only loud.

questions.q: Smash cut vs jump cut?
questions.a: A jump cut skips time inside a similar framing; a smash cut leaves for a violently different image or sound. Similarity is the jump cut's tell, contrast is the smash cut's.

questions.q: How can sound play with a smash cut?
questions.a: Either smash together with the picture, or delay it for a second hit - Oppenheimer lets the Trinity flash arrive visually before the blast sound.

items.plain: Imagine a horror movie showing a quiet, empty street for ten slow seconds. You relax. Then - SLAM - a truck horn and headlights fill the screen with no fade at all. That deliberate whiplash, where one world is yanked away for its opposite, is a smash cut.
items.image_alt: A small calm paper candle flame on the left, a huge jagged vermilion burst on the right, one hard vertical edge between them.
items.info_alt: Diagram: a long quiet grey frame with a small candle, a hard cut line, then a huge bright burst, with a small sound-wave icon arriving one step later.
items.info_caption: Hold the earned quiet - cut hard to the opposite on two axes at once - optionally let the sound land one beat later.

items.headline: 48 agents, 1,200 km2 of jungle, one hilltop
items.deck: A traveler pointed 48 AI agents at public NASA lidar of the Maya jungle; overnight they flagged a plazas-and-pyramid site missing from Mexico's official register. The twist: archaeologists had already mapped it - and that's the most useful part of the story.
items.lead: Pietro Miotti recounts how his AI agents, analyzing about 1,200 km2 of public NASA lidar over the Maya region, flagged a hilltop site with a plaza, an oval pyramid 8-12 m tall and a raised courtyard that Mexico's INAH confirmed was not in its official register - 72 hours from idea to official reply. His own November 11 update adds the honest twist: archaeologists had already mapped the site (Estrada-Belli et al. 2025); the agents had rediscovered it.
items.body: Pietro Miotti recounts how his AI agents, analyzing about 1,200 km2 of public NASA lidar over the Maya region, flagged a hilltop site with a plaza, an oval pyramid 8-12 m tall and a raised courtyard that Mexico's INAH confirmed was not in its official register - 72 hours from idea to official reply. His own November 11 update adds the honest twist: archaeologists had already mapped the site (Estrada-Belli et al. 2025); the agents had rediscovered it. The method matters more than the find. Lidar fires laser pulses through gaps in the jungle canopy and maps the ground beneath, so ruins invisible in satellite photos stand out as bare-earth geometry. The agents turned the lidar strips into images and 48 of them went through the pictures one by one, following a precise guide - no special model or classifier, just patient looking, filtering out natural hills, sinkholes and roads. They then searched the literature and archives for which candidates were unregistered, checked the raw point cloud to confirm the shapes were ground and not vegetation, drafted a report (translated into Spanish by Claude), and Miotti sent it to INAH, which replied that no registered site existed at those coordinates. The likely reading, from his long chat with the agents: a small Classic-period Maya civic centre, roughly AD 250-900 - plaza for gatherings, temple pyramid, possibly a ruler's raised courtyard, and a hollow that might be an aguada, a rainwater reservoir. The update reframes everything: the site sat in Estrada-Belli et al. 2025 but not yet in INAH's register, so the agents independently arrived where professional archaeologists already had - which Miotti reads as a good sign for the method, not a failure. Context: in 2024, archaeologists using the same kind of lidar found an entire Maya city (Auld-Thomas et al. 2024).
ptrs: What happened: 48 agents scanned ~1,200 km2 of public NASA lidar imagery overnight and flagged a hilltop with a plaza, an 8-12 m oval pyramid, a raised courtyard and a possible reservoir - absent from Mexico's INAH register.
Why lidar: laser pulses slip through canopy gaps and map bare ground - a ruin that is 'just trees' in satellite photos becomes visible geometry.
How they worked: lidar strips turned into images; 48 agents reviewed them one by one following a precise guide - no special classifier - filtering out hills, sinkholes and roads.

The verification chain: literature + archive search for unregistered candidates, raw point-cloud check (green = leaves, brown = ground), a report translated into Spanish, and INAH's official reply confirming no registered site at the location.

The twist (his Nov 11 update): the site was already mapped in Estrada-Belli et al. 2025 - the agents missed it in the literature, so this was a rediscovery, not a discovery; it just wasn't in INAH's register yet.
The reading (his speculation with the agents): a small Classic-period Maya civic centre, c. AD 250-900 - plaza, temple pyramid, elite courtyard, maybe an aguada for the dry season.
His lesson: an outsider with agents ended up where the experts did - context: archaeologists found a whole Maya city with lidar in 2024 (Auld-Thomas et al.).
items.why: This is the agent playbook at full send, bro: public data + many patient agents + a guide + verification loop = a result the government answered in 72 hours. And the twist is the real lesson - the agents' miss was skipping one paper, which is exactly the step you'll nail after reading this.
items.example: The overnight workflow, concretely: turn the lidar into images, have 48 agents walk them one by one with a written rubric (pyramids, platforms, plazas - reject hills, sinkholes, roads), then make the shortlist earn its place through literature search and a raw point-cloud check before anyone emails a government.

questions.q: Why can't satellites just photograph Maya ruins?
questions.a: From above, a ruin in the jungle is just unbroken trees. Lidar fires laser pulses through gaps in the canopy and maps the bare ground beneath, where the structures stand out.

questions.q: Did the agents use a special archaeology model?
questions.a: No - 48 general agents looked at lidar images one by one, following a precise guide for what pyramids, platforms and plazas look like versus hills, sinkholes and roads.

questions.q: Was it a real discovery?
questions.a: A rediscovery: the author's update notes archaeologists had mapped the site in Estrada-Belli et al. 2025, but it wasn't yet in INAH's register - so the agents independently landed where the experts had.

items.plain: Jungle hides ruins the way a blanket hides toys - satellites only see the blanket. Lidar is a laser that peeks under it and draws the floor. One traveler had 48 AI helpers scan those drawings overnight, and they pointed at a hilltop with a plaza and pyramid - which turned out to be a place experts had also found, just not in the official list yet.
items.image_alt: A dense paper jungle canopy parting to reveal a geometric plaza and pyramid shape in lidar colors beneath.
items.info_alt: Diagram: a satellite photo of trees struck through, an arrow to a lidar bare-ground view with a pyramid shape, arrows to a magnifying glass over a book, ending at a government envelope.
items.info_caption: Satellite sees trees - lidar strips them away - agents scan and verify - the register says unlisted, the literature says mapped.

items.headline: United to AI agents: no tickets for you
items.deck: United Airlines is banning AI agents from booking flights for travelers, citing credential risks and federal rules - while Southwest is doing the opposite and putting its inventory inside ChatGPT. The agent economy just hit its first airline wall.
items.lead: United Airlines said Wednesday it is banning AI agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing security risks and potential violations of federal rules, and is updating its booking and ticketing policies to restrict unauthorized third-party AI assistants - while rival Southwest has taken the opposite path, making its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users.
items.body: United Airlines said Wednesday it is banning AI agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing security risks and potential violations of federal rules, and is updating its booking and ticketing policies to restrict unauthorized third-party AI assistants - while rival Southwest has taken the opposite path, making its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users. United's stated reasons: an agent booking a flight needs access to a customer's personal information and payment credentials, and 'sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.' It also argues that agent actions like checking in could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage contains no banned substances. The restrictions will be enforced directly on United's platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators. Analyst Henry Harteveldt of Atmosphere Research Group reads a business motive underneath: United wants to avoid adding 'yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary' alongside Google search, metasearch and online travel agencies - and AI bot flight searches themselves cost airlines money. Consumers can still book United fares through aggregators like Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights. Meanwhile consumers are increasingly turning to AI agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots for tasks from product research to purchases, so this fight is arriving everywhere at once.
ptrs: The move: United is banning third-party personal AI agents from booking flights for travelers, updating booking and ticketing policies, and restricting access directly on its platforms and indirectly via agencies and aggregators.
Stated reason one: credential sharing with AI assistants can expose sensitive information and lead to unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.
Stated reason two: agent actions like check-in could violate federal rules - e.g., the requirement that travelers verify in person that luggage holds no banned substances.
Analyst read (Henry Harteveldt, Atmosphere Research): United wants to avoid another powerful intermediary beyond Google search, metasearch and OTAs - and AI bot flight searches cost airlines money.
The split: Southwest is going the other way - its flight inventory is viewable inside ChatGPT. United fares stay bookable via Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights.
The backdrop: consumers are adopting agents like Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots for research, deals and purchases - so booking is the first big consumer arena to pick a side.
items.why: You're literally building in the agent era, bro, and this is its first big consumer boundary: some giants will bolt the door, some will build a side entrance for agents. Watching who picks which door tells you where the agent-friendly opportunities will be.
items.example: Same trip, two futures: ask your agent for a flight to Delhi - under United's policy the agent must stop at the booking button and hand it back to you; on Southwest's approach the agent can show you the inventory inside the chat. One industry, two opposite bets, decided this week.

questions.q: What exactly did United ban?
questions.a: Unauthorized third-party personal AI agents making flight reservations on behalf of travelers - enforced on its own platforms and via travel agencies and aggregators.

questions.q: What reasons did United give?
questions.a: Security risks from sharing account credentials and payment info with AI assistants (unintended purchases, account changes, miles usage), plus possible violations of federal rules like in-person luggage verification.

questions.q: Are other airlines doing the same?
questions.a: No - Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, the opposite tack; and United fares remain bookable through Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights.

items.plain: Booking a flight means handing over your card and confirming safety questions - United says only you should do that, not your AI helper. Another airline disagrees and lets the AI show you its flights. The agents-versus-gatekeepers match has officially kicked off.
items.image_alt: A paper airplane meeting a raised stop-hand shape at a gate, while a second airplane flies through an open gate nearby.

items.headline: Build on AWS without touching AWS
items.deck: AWS quietly open-sourced an official local emulator of its own APIs: run it on your machine, point the AWS CLI at localhost, and test cloud code with zero account, zero bill, zero deploys. Windows runs it in a small Docker container.
items.lead: AWS Emulator is AWS's own open-source (CC0) local emulator of the AWS APIs: you test your software against emulated resources on your machine, a dev server, or CI - no AWS account needed, no service fee, requests never leave your machine. It's written in Rust, ships as a local program serving an AWS API endpoint, and on Windows or macOS you run it in a container built from a short Dockerfile.
items.body: AWS Emulator is AWS's own open-source (CC0) local emulator of the AWS APIs: you test your software against emulated resources on your machine, a dev server, or CI - no AWS account needed, no service fee, requests never leave your machine. It's written in Rust, ships as a local program serving an AWS API endpoint, and on Windows or macOS you run it in a container built from a short Dockerfile. How it works: start the emulator, set environment variables so the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK points at its local endpoint (HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 with a self-signed certificate), then run your code as usual - you're now working with emulated resources instead of AWS resources. Rust projects get a second mode, embedded: add the emulator as a dev-dependency and run it in-process, one isolated instance per test, with no endpoint or certificates to manage. There's even an official AI-agent path: install the aws-emulator skill and ask your coding agent to set it up (needs AWS CLI 2.35.0+). The honest caveats: it's for building and testing, not production workloads or security testing; emulation fidelity varies by service - each release publishes fidelity scores, and gaps are tracked in the repo's issues directory. The natural comparison is LocalStack, the established third-party AWS emulator whose fuller features sit behind paid tiers; AWS Emulator is the official, fully free entrant - newer, so check the fidelity scores for the services you need before committing a project to it. The project appeared in September 2026 and already sits around 2k stars.
ptrs: What it is: AWS's official open-source (CC0) local emulator of the AWS APIs, written in Rust - test cloud code with no AWS account and no service fee; you pay only when you actually deploy on AWS.
How you use it: run the local program, point the AWS CLI or SDK at its endpoint (HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, self-signed cert) via environment variables, run your code unchanged.
Windows/macOS path: a short Dockerfile builds a container that runs the emulator; Linux gets native RPM/Debian packages.
Rust bonus: embedded mode compiles it into your test binary - one isolated instance per test, no endpoints to manage.
Agent path: an official aws-emulator skill lets your coding agent do the setup (requires AWS CLI 2.35.0 or later).
Caveats: not for production or security testing; fidelity varies per service - check the published fidelity scores and the issues/ directory before relying on a given API.
Vs LocalStack: the established third-party emulator gates fuller features behind paid tiers; this one is official and entirely free, but newer - verify the services you need.
items.why: Cloud tutorials always end with a credit card form, bro - this kills that. You can learn S3-style workflows, break things, and run the whole experiment loop on localhost for zero rupees, and your coding agent can even set it up for you.
items.example: Tonight's drill, Windows edition: install Docker Desktop, build the emulator's short Dockerfile, run the container, then set the AWS CLI's endpoint env vars to https://127.0.0.1:9297 and run your usual commands - they now hit the emulator, not Amazon. Check the release fidelity scores for the services you try.

questions.q: Do I need an AWS account or card?
questions.a: No - requests go to the emulator on your own machine, not to AWS. There's no account and no service fee; you pay only for real AWS resources when you deploy for real.

questions.q: How do I run it on Windows?
questions.a: Run it in a container built from the short Dockerfile in the docs (Linux gets native packages instead). Then point your CLI or SDK at the local endpoint with environment variables.

questions.q: Is it a full fake AWS?
questions.a: No - fidelity varies by service and it's meant for building and testing, not production or security testing. Each release publishes fidelity scores and the repo tracks known gaps.

items.plain: It's a flight simulator for the cloud. Your code talks to a pretend AWS running on your own computer - same commands, same responses - so you can practice takeoffs and landings with no airport, no ticket, and no way to crash anything real.
