items.headline: Thinking longer isn't thinking better
items.deck: A sharp new mental model: a reasoning model isn't walking one road to the answer - it's rolling dice on thousands of paths and hoping one lands. That single idea explains overthinking, best-of-k wins, and why chains of thought can lie.
items.lead: A widely-shared post by researcher Alex Wang reframes reasoning models as pathfinders in token space: the prompt is a starting point, the correct answers form a target zone, and each chain of thought is one sampled path trying to land in it. This picture explains a real puzzle - models trained with RL write longer chains and get more accurate, yet forcing any single chain to run longer helps for a while, then stops helping and can even make answers worse.
items.body: A widely-shared post by researcher Alex Wang reframes reasoning models as pathfinders in token space: the prompt is a starting point, the correct answers form a target zone, and each chain of thought is one sampled path trying to land in it. This picture explains a real puzzle - models trained with RL write longer chains and get more accurate, yet forcing any single chain to run longer helps for a while, then stops helping and can even make answers worse. Formally: given prompt x, the model samples a path z; a verifier r(x, y) returns 1 if the final answer y is correct; the goal is to land in S_x, the set of correct answers. The success probability p_x is just the summed probability of every path that lands in S_x - which is exactly the expected binary reward that RL with verifiable rewards maximizes. Two consequences follow. First, best-of-k sampling is a guaranteed axis of improvement: sample k paths and the chance at least one lands is 1 - (1 - p_x)^k, which rises monotonically with k - more samples always help, unlike longer chains. Second, RL turns out to be rejection-sampling fine-tuning on the model's own paths, scaled by the success rate: sample paths, keep the ones that landed, train on them, repeat. Chains get longer during training only because the paths that succeeded tended to be longer (they backtrack, gather more feedback), not because length is the objective. The model then amortizes the search - it pays the compute once in training so it can produce good paths directly, generalizing to new prompts with accuracy falling off as prompts drift from the training distribution. The frame also demystifies two odd behaviors: chains of thought need not be faithful, because the verifier only checks the final answer, not whether the intermediate steps are true; and reward hacking appears when the verifier is imperfect, because the accepted set then includes wrong answers the model learns to aim for.
ptrs: The model: prompt x is a start point, the chain of thought z is a sampled path, a verifier r(x, y) marks the landing correct or not, and the win set S_x holds every correct answer.
The post's own example: 'what is 1 + 2 + ... + 10?' Path one adds one at a time; path two pairs outside-in (1+10, 2+9, ... five 11s). Different paths, same landing: 55.

The puzzle it solves: RL-trained models write longer chains and improve - but stretch ONE chain and gains plateau then reverse, as if overthinking. If each chain converged to an optimum, longer should never hurt.
Best-of-k is the guaranteed lever: the chance at least one of k sampled paths lands is 1 - (1 - p_x)^k - monotonic in k, so more samples always help (a compute axis that is not chain length).

RL with verifiable rewards = rejection-sampling fine-tuning scaled by the current success rate: sample paths, keep landers, train on them, repeat. Chains lengthen only because successful paths happened to be longer.
Amortization: training pays the search cost once so the model emits good paths directly; it generalizes to unseen prompts, with accuracy dropping the further the prompt drifts from training data.
Two demystified quirks: chains need not be faithful (the verifier only scores the answer), and reward hacking is what happens when the verifier accepts wrong answers into S_x.
items.why: This is the cleanest answer yet to 'what did RL actually do to make models smart?', bro - and it's immediately usable: when an answer matters, sample the model several times and check, because best-of-k always helps, while begging it to 'think longer' has an expiry date.
items.example: Ask a reasoning model the same hard aptitude question five times. You'll often get five different chains - some landing right, some wandering off. The post's math says that spread is the point: your job is to sample enough paths and verify the landings, not to stretch one path until it breaks.

questions.q: If thinking longer isn't the objective, what is?
questions.a: Landing in the set of correct answers S_x. Training maximizes the probability that a sampled path lands there; chain length is just a side effect of which paths succeeded.

questions.q: Why does best-of-k sampling always help?
questions.a: Each path misses with probability (1 - p_x), so all k miss with probability (1 - p_x)^k - success is 1 minus that, which only grows as k grows.

questions.q: Why can a chain of thought be unfaithful?
questions.a: The verifier only checks the final answer. Nothing in the reward requires the intermediate tokens to be true or to explain the answer that follows.

items.plain: Imagine a maze with many routes to the exit. A reasoning model doesn't walk one perfect route - it tries thousands of random walks and some reach the exit. Training means remembering which corridors worked. Sending ten walkers always raises the odds someone exits; forcing one walker to keep walking after they found it just tires them out.
items.image_alt: A paper maze with several dotted wandering paths, a few reaching a vermilion star zone, others dead-ending.
items.info_alt: Diagram: one dot on the left, several meandering arrows, some landing inside a marked zone on the right, others missing it.
items.info_caption: Each arrow is one sampled chain of thought: some land in the correct zone, some miss - training raises the odds.

items.headline: Your phone videos are now 3D scenes
items.deck: Blender 5.3 lands native Gaussian splat support: film a place on your phone, reconstruct it as millions of soft glowing blobs, and render it inside the same free, open-source 3D suite the pros use. Paid suites like Cinema 4D and Maya charge subscriptions; Blender charges nothing.
items.lead: Blender 5.3 is out, and its headline feature is native 3D Gaussian Splatting support: splats - the technique that rebuilds 3D scenes from ordinary photos or video as clouds of tiny soft transparent blobs - can now be imported, processed and rendered directly inside Blender, the free and open-source 3D suite.
items.body: Blender 5.3 is out, and its headline feature is native 3D Gaussian Splatting support: splats - the technique that rebuilds 3D scenes from ordinary photos or video as clouds of tiny soft transparent blobs - can now be imported, processed and rendered directly inside Blender, the free and open-source 3D suite. Concretely, Blender imports splats from PLY, SPZ and glTF files, stores them as point clouds with special attributes (scale, rotation, base radiance and spherical-harmonics coefficients), lets you process them with Geometry Nodes, preview them in Workbench, and render natively in EEVEE or Cycles. By default a splat renders with an emissive shader, and there's rudimentary relighting support by swapping in a Diffuse BSDF. Two honest caveats from the release notes: performance is still being optimized, and renders can show color inaccuracies where low opacity meets high radiance because most splat authoring tools work in sRGB while Blender works in linear color. The rest of 5.3 is stacked too: the Principled BSDF gains dispersion (glass and diamonds splitting white light into rainbows, matching OpenPBR v1.1.1), DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction arrives as a denoiser promising Cycles looks with EEVEE responsiveness (it needs an NVIDIA card with driver version 620 or newer), the Shader Editor gets per-light Material Lighting nodes, and the video editor picks up ripple editing. For your rig specifically: the DLSS denoiser is the one feature with a hard requirement - an NVIDIA RTX card with driver 620+, which your 4050 satisfies after a driver update; splat preview in Workbench (solid mode) is the light way to start.
ptrs: What shipped: Blender 5.3 with native Gaussian splat support - import PLY, SPZ or glTF, store as point clouds, edit with Geometry Nodes, render in EEVEE, Cycles or Workbench.
What a splat is: many small, soft, transparent blobs that combine to represent complex geometry and shading - commonly reconstructed from photos or videos of a real place.
The nerdy bit: each splat carries scale, rotation, base radiance plus opacity, and spherical-harmonics coefficients for view-dependent color.

Caveats (from the release notes): performance still being optimized; color inaccuracies possible where low opacity meets high radiance (sRGB authoring tools vs Blender's linear color); relighting is rudimentary via a Diffuse BSDF swap.
Also in 5.3: Principled BSDF dispersion (rainbows in glass, OpenPBR v1.1.1), DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction denoising, per-light Material Lighting nodes, ripple video editing, Outliner sorting.
Your PC check: DLSS denoising requires an NVIDIA card with driver 620 or newer - your RTX 4050 qualifies with an updated driver; Blender itself is a free download for Windows.
Cost comparison: Cinema 4D and Maya are subscription products; Blender is free and open source, and it's the same suite studios use.
items.why: Creator gold, bro: film your room, a chai stall, a campus corner on your phone, and it becomes a 3D asset you can orbit, relight and drop into renders - with software that costs zero rupees. This is the kind of visual that makes a reel stop the scroll.
items.example: The release shows the flow with Blender Studio's DOGWALK splat: a PLY file imported straight into a scene as a point cloud, then rendered. Your version: record a slow walk-around video of an object, reconstruct it with a splat tool, import the PLY into Blender 5.3, preview it in Workbench solid mode, then render in EEVEE.

questions.q: What file formats can Blender 5.3 import splats from?
questions.a: PLY, SPZ and glTF - stored as point clouds you can process with Geometry Nodes and render in EEVEE, Cycles or Workbench.

questions.q: What is a Gaussian splat, in one line?
questions.a: A cloud of many small, soft, transparent blobs that together reconstruct a real scene's geometry and shading, usually captured from photos or video.

questions.q: Does anything in 5.3 need specific hardware?
questions.a: The DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction denoiser requires an NVIDIA card with driver version 620 or newer; everything else, including splat import and EEVEE preview, runs as a normal free Blender install.

items.plain: Take dozens of photos of your desk from every angle. Software can turn them into a cloud of millions of tiny glowing dots that, together, look exactly like your desk in 3D. Blender 5.3 is the first time the free 3D program everyone uses can open, edit and render those dot-clouds directly.
items.image_alt: A paper teapot assembled from many soft overlapping translucent blobs in cobalt, vermilion and amber.
items.info_alt: Diagram: three small photos of a mug from different angles, an arrow into a cloud of soft blobs, an arrow into a solid 3D mug.
items.info_caption: Photos from many angles become millions of soft blobs; together they render as a solid 3D scene.

items.headline: The insert: cinema's magnifying glass
items.deck: Cut from the wide shot to the clock, the letter, the trembling key - that's an insert: a detail already inside the master shot, re-framed so you can't miss it. It's a Wonderful Life used two in one scene back in 1946.
items.lead: An insert is a shot of part of a scene, filmed from a different angle or focal length than the master shot. It covers action the master already covers, but the tighter framing emphasizes one detail - and that is exactly what separates it from a cutaway, which shows action the master does not cover.
items.body: An insert is a shot of part of a scene, filmed from a different angle or focal length than the master shot. It covers action the master already covers, but the tighter framing emphasizes one detail - and that is exactly what separates it from a cutaway, which shows action the master does not cover. Directors use inserts to drag the viewer's eye to a story-relevant detail that a wider shot would let slip by: a clock, a letter, a newspaper headline, an object being handled. Terminology trivia: when the new framing shows actors, it gets its own name - close-up, head shot, two shot - so 'insert' is usually reserved for objects and for body parts other than the head. Production trivia: inserts are often filmed separately from the main action, by a second-unit director working with stand-ins. And they are genuinely vexatious to shoot: to preserve continuity, the objects must sit in the same relative positions as in the main take, under the same lighting, or the splice shows. The classic citation: It's a Wonderful Life (1946) drops two inserts into one sequence - one of a sign, one of a record player - to add visual detail to the action.
ptrs: Definition: a shot of part of a scene, taken from a different angle and/or focal length than the master shot, emphasizing a different aspect of action the master already covers.
Insert vs cutaway: a cutaway covers action NOT present in the master shot; an insert re-frames action that is.
What it's for: forcing attention onto a story-relevant detail - a clock, a letter, a headline, an object in hand - that a wide shot would bury.
Naming: other views of actors get their own terms (close-up, head shot, two shot), so 'insert' usually means objects, or body parts other than the head.
How it's made: often shot separately, by a second-unit director with stand-ins - and continuity is the pain: same object positions, same lighting, or the cut shows.
The classic example: It's a Wonderful Life (1946) uses two inserts in one sequence - a sign and a record player.
items.why: This is the cheapest storytelling upgrade for your reels, bro: one tight shot of the cup, the keyboard, the ticket - and the audience knows exactly where to look. Master the insert and your edits stop feeling like random chopping.
items.example: Shoot a 20-second 'making chai' clip wide (your master). Then reshoot just the cardamom hitting the pan, tight, from a different angle. Cut wide-tight-wide. That middle shot is an insert - and you'll feel how it directs attention without a single word.

questions.q: What makes an insert different from a cutaway?
questions.a: An insert re-frames action already covered by the master shot to emphasize a detail; a cutaway shows action the master shot does not cover.

questions.q: Why not just call it a close-up?
questions.a: Views of actors have their own terms (close-up, head shot, two shot). 'Insert' is usually reserved for objects - or body parts other than the head.

questions.q: Why are inserts hard to shoot?
questions.a: Continuity: objects must hold the same relative positions under the same lighting as the main take, or the splice is visible - and they're often filmed separately with stand-ins.

items.plain: You're watching a wide shot of a kitchen and the story needs you to notice the gas flame is still on. The film cuts to a tight shot of just the flame for one second, then returns to the wide. That tight shot is an insert - same scene, different framing, one detail underlined.
items.image_alt: A wide paper frame of a desk scene beside a small tight frame of just an envelope, with an arrow zooming between them.
items.info_alt: Diagram: a large frame showing a whole room, an arrow into a small frame showing one letter in detail, an arrow returning to the large frame.
items.info_caption: Master shot - insert on the one detail that matters - back to the master. The cutaway, by contrast, leaves the scene.

items.headline: AI just proved Signal's code keeps its secrets
items.deck: Google DeepMind's new AlphaProof Code framework guided agents to mathematically verify the actual code behind the Signal protocol - a grand challenge in security - writing over six million lines of machine-checked proof in four weeks, a job that historically takes expert teams years.
items.lead: Google DeepMind announced AlphaProof Code, an agentic framework that formally verified the code underlying the Signal protocol - the cryptography protecting billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. DeepMind says it's the first time AI has formally verified a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth, and the first time the implementation of such a protocol has been formally verified by any method at all.
items.body: Google DeepMind announced AlphaProof Code, an agentic framework that formally verified the code underlying the Signal protocol - the cryptography protecting billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. DeepMind says it's the first time AI has formally verified a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth, and the first time the implementation of such a protocol has been formally verified by any method at all. Formal verification - mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws - is the highest standard of security assurance, and most earlier protocol verification stopped at the design level; this work goes down to the compiled code, proving properties like keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised. The framework splits work like a research team: human experts worked with a mix of models to translate Signal's security goals into formal mathematical specifications, reviewing every one; then agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proving, generating over six million lines of Lean, a language a computer can check line by line. The agents then audited their own proof and flagged just one percent of the codebase for human re-review - because Lean automatically checks the rest, human judgment lands only where it matters most. The whole verification took four weeks. As a sanity check, the team reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code; in both cases the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure. Signal CTO Ehren Kret called it a major breakthrough. DeepMind is open-sourcing the verification artifacts and pitches the approach as groundwork for verifying medical firmware and power-grid software next.
ptrs: The claim: DeepMind's AlphaProof Code formally verified the actual code of the Signal protocol - first AI verification of a widely deployed crypto protocol at this depth, and first implementation-level verification of one by any method.
Why implementation-level matters: real vulnerabilities hide in the gap between design and code; this proof covers the exact compiled code running on devices.

The pipeline: humans + models write formal specs (every one human-reviewed); Gemini Carbon agents generate 6M+ lines of Lean proofs; agents audit and flag ~1% of the codebase for human second look; Lean machine-checks everything.
What was proved: key security properties hold - including messages staying protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised.
Speed: four weeks, against a task DeepMind says historically takes expert teams years.
Validation: two real previously-fixed bugs reintroduced into an isolated copy were both machine-proven insecure.
What's next: artifacts are being open-sourced with a technical paper; DeepMind points at medical devices and power-grid software, paired with defense agents like CodeMender.
items.why: Remember the Fermat formalization from yesterday's issue? Same family, bro - but this one guards real messages on real phones today. Watch the pattern: AI as proof-writer plus a machine gatekeeper that never gets tired. That's a career shape, not just a headline.
items.example: The trust trick in one move: the agents wrote six million lines of proof, but nobody had to trust the agents - the Lean checker verified every line mechanically, and humans spent their attention on the 1% the agents themselves flagged as worth a second look.

questions.q: What is formal verification?
questions.a: Mathematically proving that code runs correctly without flaws - the highest standard of security assurance, here expressed in the Lean proof language that a computer checks line by line.

questions.q: What did the AI agents actually do?
questions.a: After humans approved the formal specs, Gemini Carbon agents generated over six million lines of Lean proof and audited it, flagging about 1% of the codebase for human re-review.

questions.q: How do we know the system isn't just rubber-stamping?
questions.a: The team reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated copy of Signal's code - in both cases the framework produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure.

items.plain: Normally you trust an app's security because smart people checked it. Here, AI agents wrote out a gigantic mathematical proof that Signal's code does what it promises - and a separate, simple computer program checked every line of that proof. Humans only had to re-read the 1% the agents circled as tricky.
items.image_alt: A paper padlock with a keyhole standing guard over two abstract speech-bubble shapes, with a tiny checkmark seal.
items.info_alt: Diagram of three stages: a document with a seal, a stack of proof lines with agent gears, and a gatekeeper checkmark with a small magnifying glass over a thin slice.
items.info_caption: Spec approved by humans - agents write 6M lines of machine-checked proof - Lean gatekeeps, humans re-read the flagged 1%.

items.headline: 37,966 findings, 217 fixes: the receipts
items.deck: Seven months after Anthropic's Project Glasswing launched with 'thousands of high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities', VulnCheck's tracker counts 442 CVEs, two exploited in the wild, and a fix count of 217 - while curl's maintainer marked 19 of 34 published reports as not vulnerabilities.
items.lead: VulnCheck's Patrick Garrity has published a seven-month receipt-check on Anthropic's Project Glasswing: his tracker attributes 442 CVEs to Anthropic (about 0.5% of the 93,450 CVEs published this year), only two of them exploited in the wild, while Anthropic's own ledger lists 37,966 findings with just 217 marked fixed. The freshest reality check comes from curl, where maintainer Daniel Stenberg published Anthropic's scanner reports: of 34 published so far, 19 are marked not a vulnerability, 6 confirmed low severity, and 9 await assessment.
items.body: VulnCheck's Patrick Garrity has published a seven-month receipt-check on Anthropic's Project Glasswing: his tracker attributes 442 CVEs to Anthropic (about 0.5% of the 93,450 CVEs published this year), only two of them exploited in the wild, while Anthropic's own ledger lists 37,966 findings with just 217 marked fixed. The freshest reality check comes from curl, where maintainer Daniel Stenberg published Anthropic's scanner reports: of 34 published so far, 19 are marked not a vulnerability, 6 confirmed low severity, and 9 await assessment. Glasswing launched on April 7 claiming thousands of high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities being responsibly disclosed. Garrity's ledger math: only 7,349 findings (19.4%) have been made public; 1,654 (4.4%) are marked duplicates - nearly eight times the fix count - and 419 withdrawn; since September 8 the ledger added 11,813 findings and only 15 fixes, while the claimed true positive rate rose from 90.8% to 94.2%, which he questions given the duplicate and withdrawal pile-up. Anthropic's October pivot is the OSS Scanner: projects opt in and triage findings themselves, with Anthropic upfront that reports are 'fully model-generated, without human review or triage' and may be 'incorrect or invalid' - after admitting it had manually reviewed only about 6,000 of 29,000+ candidates and was 'bottlenecked on human capacity'. curl's numbers so far imply a 55.9% false positive rate and a 17.6% confirmation rate, all low severity - versus that claimed 94.2% - and back in May, five Mythos findings boiled down to a single confirmed vulnerability. In September, Garrity found Claude rated 91.5% of ledger findings critical or high where maintainers rated 51.3%. His takeaway is measured, not dismissive: AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities - but the launch narrative still doesn't reconcile with the receipts, and curl's choice to publish everything openly is the transparency model to copy.
ptrs: The tracker (VulnCheck's Patrick Garrity, seven months in): 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic - about 0.5% of this year's 93,450 - with only 2 exploited in the wild (0.45%).
Anthropic's ledger: 37,966 findings, 7,349 (19.4%) public, 217 fixed, 1,654 duplicates (about 7.5x the fixes), 419 withdrawn - and a claimed true positive rate that rose to 94.2%.
The two-month trend: +11,813 findings, +15 fixes since September 8.

The pivot: the OSS Scanner lets maintainers opt in and triage themselves - 'fully model-generated, without human review or triage', and reports may be 'incorrect or invalid'. The triage bottleneck moved to maintainers.

curl's reality check (Daniel Stenberg): 45 reports received; of 34 published so far - 19 not vulnerabilities, 6 confirmed low severity, 9 pending. That's a 55.9% false positive rate, 17.6% confirmed, all low. In May, five Mythos findings became one confirmed vuln.
Severity gap from September: Claude rated 91.5% of ledger findings critical/high; maintainers rated 51.3% that way.

Fair framing: Garrity himself says AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities - his argument is that the evidence doesn't match the launch marketing, and curl's full-transparency publishing is the model to follow.
items.why: This is your media-literacy protein, bro: a huge 'AI finds thousands of critical bugs' headline, and one patient nerd with a spreadsheet checking the receipts seven months later. When you ship your own AI projects someday, this is the audit you'll want to survive.
items.example: curl's maintainer received 45 scanner reports and is publishing them at a deliberate pace 'to soften the impact for the team'. So far: 19 rejected, 6 confirmed low, 9 pending - a concrete look at what '94.2% true positive' meets when a human maintainer actually grades the homework.

questions.q: What did Project Glasswing claim at launch?
questions.a: On April 7, Anthropic said it had identified thousands of high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities being responsibly disclosed to open source maintainers.

questions.q: What do the ledger numbers show after seven months?
questions.a: 37,966 findings, 19.4% made public, 217 fixed, 1,654 duplicates and 419 withdrawn - with +11,813 findings but only +15 fixes in the last two months.

questions.q: What happened when curl graded the scanner's reports?
questions.a: Of 34 reports published so far, 19 were marked not a vulnerability, 6 confirmed as low severity, and 9 are awaiting assessment - a 55.9% false positive rate so far, versus the claimed 94.2% true positive rate.

items.plain: Imagine a classmate who announces they found 38,000 mistakes in the school's books. Seven months later, someone checks: only 217 mistakes got fixed, a pile turned out to be duplicates, and when a librarian graded the latest batch, over half weren't mistakes at all. Finding mistakes fast is still useful - but the boast and the scoreboard tell different stories.

items.headline: De-2019 your coding agent tonight
items.deck: Google Chrome's team open-sourced Modern Web Guidance: a free CLI that feeds current web-platform best practices straight into your coding agent, steering it off legacy JavaScript patterns and onto native modern APIs. One npx command, no install, works on Windows.
items.lead: Modern Web Guidance is an open-source (Apache 2.0) set of skills that embeds web-platform expertise, best practices and browser-compatibility data directly into coding agents - stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox and MDN teams. It exists because LLM training data is stuffed with legacy code, so agents keep generating bloated JavaScript for things the modern web platform now does natively.
items.body: Modern Web Guidance is an open-source (Apache 2.0) set of skills that embeds web-platform expertise, best practices and browser-compatibility data directly into coding agents - stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox and MDN teams. It exists because LLM training data is stuffed with legacy code, so agents keep generating bloated JavaScript for things the modern web platform now does natively. The CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines into your agent's context window across three focus areas: modern browser APIs (correctly structuring APIs models frequently misuse), performance and accessibility (platform-level APIs the browser can optimize, with built-in accessibility), and responsible fallbacks (lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries). You don't even need to install it to try it: 'npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop"' searches relevant guides, 'retrieve' fetches a guide by ID, and 'legacy-scan .' scans a codebase for legacy patterns worth modernizing. 'npx modern-web-guidance@latest install' runs an interactive wizard to wire it into your agent setup permanently. The repo sits at about 3.2k stars, and the one-time cost is zero - it's a free utility from the browser teams themselves.
ptrs: What it is: a free, Apache-2.0 set of agent 'skills' feeding modern web best practices and browser-compat data into coding agents - stewarded by the Chrome, Edge, Firefox and MDN teams.

Why it exists: LLM training data is full of legacy code, so agents default to old patterns and bloated JS for tasks that now have native, high-performance platform solutions - and even when a model knows an API, it often lacks dense real-world modern patterns.

Three focus areas: modern browser APIs (fixed structure for commonly misused APIs), performance + accessibility (native platform features), and responsible fallbacks (lightweight, not heavy polyfills).
Try without installing: npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop" to find guides; retrieve a guide by ID; legacy-scan . to audit a codebase.
Install for keeps: npx modern-web-guidance@latest install runs an interactive wizard.
Tonight's drill: open a terminal in any web project, run the legacy-scan, and let your agent fix one finding using the retrieved guide - about ten minutes, zero cost, needs only Node/npm.
items.why: You build sites with coding agents all the time, bro - including this newspaper. Agents write the JavaScript they learned from a decade of Stack Overflow; this pipes the browser teams' current playbook into the context window so the code comes out modern, leaner and more accessible. Free upgrade, ten minutes.
items.example: Run 'npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan .' inside any project folder. It lists legacy patterns in your code; pick one, 'retrieve' the matching guide, paste it to your agent, and watch a jQuery-era pattern become a native API call.

questions.q: What problem does Modern Web Guidance solve?
questions.a: Coding agents trained on legacy-heavy data generate outdated, bloated JavaScript for tasks the modern platform now handles natively; the CLI injects expert-curated current guidance into the agent's context.

questions.q: Do I have to install anything to try it?
questions.a: No - npx modern-web-guidance@latest search/retrieve/legacy-scan all run directly; the install command is only for wiring it in permanently via a wizard.

questions.q: Who maintains it and what does it cost?
questions.a: It's open source (Apache 2.0), stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox and MDN teams - free.

items.plain: Your AI helper learned to code from the whole internet - including tutorials from 2015. So it keeps solving problems the old, clunky way. This tool is like handing it today's official manual first: 'here's how browsers do it now' - and suddenly the code gets shorter and better.

items.headline: The k-means from your textbook just got lapped
items.deck: Meta's FAIR lab open-sourced e-means, a drop-in replacement for the k-means update rule that reaches the classic algorithm's 25-epoch quality in 1.2 to 3 epochs - 10 to 45 times less wall-clock time on GPU - with zero hyperparameters to tune.
items.lead: e-means is a newly open-sourced k-means algorithm from Meta FAIR that replaces Lloyd's algorithm, the update rule behind nearly every k-means you have ever run. It reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs in just 1.2 to 3 epochs, measured 10-45x faster end-to-end than Flash-KMeans (the fastest GPU Lloyd implementation) and 8-15x faster than Faiss on CPU, while needing no hyperparameter tuning at all.
items.body: e-means is a newly open-sourced k-means algorithm from Meta FAIR that replaces Lloyd's algorithm, the update rule behind nearly every k-means you have ever run. It reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs in just 1.2 to 3 epochs, measured 10-45x faster end-to-end than Flash-KMeans (the fastest GPU Lloyd implementation) and 8-15x faster than Faiss on CPU, while needing no hyperparameter tuning at all. The core swap is the update rule. Lloyd recomputes each cluster's centroid as the exact mean of every point assigned to it, which costs one full pass over the dataset, repeated 20 to 50 times. e-means instead works on mini-batches and keeps an exponential moving average of each cluster's sum and count: every small batch nudges the centroid, and older assignments fade away at a rate called alpha, so the centroid tracks recent points instead of the whole history. Around that rule sit a novel initialization, a dead-cluster revival trick (small clusters get revived by splitting a large one), a cosine schedule that anneals alpha like a learning rate, and a cheap finalization pass that ends on each cluster's exact mean. The team also derived scaling laws that automatically pick the batch size and step size, which is why there is nothing to tune. Two results in the write-up are worth pausing on. First: set the batch to the full dataset and alpha to 1, and e-means becomes exactly Lloyd's algorithm - the classic method is just the extreme corner case, and the team's loss map shows that corner sits 1.8% above the best setting. Second: they chose moving averages over gradient descent because the average keeps each centroid inside the convex hull of its assigned points, while gradient steps can overshoot - at its best setting, gradient descent still ended 0.4-1.6% above the moving average. The name e-means comes from those exponential moving averages.
ptrs: Quick recap: k-means takes n points and an integer k, and hunts for k centroids that minimize the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid.

The classic solver, Lloyd's algorithm: assign every point to its nearest centroid, recompute each centroid as the exact mean of its points, repeat 20-50 times. Every round costs one full sweep over the data.

e-means' swap: mini-batches plus an exponential moving average. Each small batch updates every cluster's running sum and count, and the centroid is just their ratio; old assignments fade at rate alpha.
Nothing to tune: batch size and step size are set automatically by scaling laws the team derived, and a cosine schedule anneals alpha down to a tenth of its start, like a learning rate.
Extras in the box: a better initialization, dead-cluster revival (tiny clusters get revived by splitting a big one), and a finalization pass that ends on exact means for a negligible time cost.
The numbers: Lloyd's 25-epoch loss matched or beaten in 1.2-3 epochs; 10-45x less wall-clock than Flash-KMeans on GPU; 8-15x less than Faiss on CPU.
Lloyd is a special case: full batch plus alpha = 1 makes one e-means step exactly one Lloyd step - and that extreme corner is 1.8% above the best loss on the team's hyperparameter map.
Why not gradient descent? The moving average keeps each centroid inside the convex hull of its assigned points; gradient steps can overshoot the hull and proved unstable at large learning rates.
Built at Meta FAIR and open-sourced; it is highly parallelizable and ships with specialized kernels that turn the epoch savings into real wall-clock savings.
items.why: K-means is probably the first clustering algorithm you ever met, and the version everyone teaches is a 1967 update rule. This is a rare case where the textbook answer genuinely changed this week, bro - knowing why mini-batches plus fading memory beat the full-pass classic is exactly the kind of thing that separates 'ran sklearn once' from 'understands the algorithm'.
items.example: Picture compressing a photo down to 16 colors - that is k-means over pixels. Lloyd sweeps every pixel in the image up to 25 times to settle the palette. e-means grabs small batches of pixels, keeps a fading running average per color, and lands a palette of the same quality in about 3 sweeps' worth of work.

questions.q: What is a centroid?
questions.a: Each cluster's center point. Every cluster keeps a running sum and a count of its points, and the centroid is simply sum divided by count - the mean position.

questions.q: What does the exponential moving average actually do?
questions.a: Instead of recomputing each cluster's statistics from scratch over the whole dataset, each mini-batch blends in: new stats = (1 - alpha) x old + alpha x batch. Older batches fade exponentially, so the centroid tracks recent assignments.

questions.q: Do I need to tune batch size or step size?
questions.a: No - that is one of the headline claims. The team derived scaling laws that set both automatically from the data's scale, which previous mini-batch k-means methods never managed.

items.plain: Imagine re-seating a hall of a thousand students into 20 groups. Lloyd's way: after every shuffle, recount the ENTIRE hall before moving anyone - 25 full recounts. e-means' way: check small batches, keep a fading running tally per group, and let recent placements count more. You reach a better seating plan in about 3 batches' worth of work, and nobody had to tell you the batch size - a formula picked it.

items.headline: 60-30-10: the recipe behind every calm palette
items.deck: One dominant color for 60% of the canvas, a secondary for 30%, a loud accent for 10% - the classic interior-design ratio that keeps interfaces balanced and makes the one button that matters impossible to miss.
items.lead: The 60-30-10 rule divides a design's color usage into three shares: 60% for a dominant color that sets the overall tone (usually the background), 30% for a secondary color that adds contrast and interest in smaller areas, and 10% for a vibrant accent reserved for key elements like call-to-action buttons.
items.body: The 60-30-10 rule divides a design's color usage into three shares: 60% for a dominant color that sets the overall tone (usually the background), 30% for a secondary color that adds contrast and interest in smaller areas, and 10% for a vibrant accent reserved for key elements like call-to-action buttons. The dominant 60% is typically neutral or low-saturation so it never overpowers; the secondary 30% complements it on sidebars, cards and secondary sections; the accent 10% is the most vibrant color on the screen, used sparingly so it always reads as 'this is the thing to press'. The rule is functional, not just aesthetic: the ratio guides the user's eye through the interface, highlights what is important, and builds a visual hierarchy that makes a screen feel navigable before anyone reads a word. It also bends by style. In neobrutalism, the heavy black outlines around cards and buttons act as the 10% accent, with the backdrop as dominant and high-contrast components as secondary. In soft, minimal neumorphism, the background is a quiet neutral at 60%, cards and panels form the 30%, and the accent shows up in small interactive elements, subtle shadows and highlights. The ratio even rhymes with column grids: main content fills the largest central share, a sidebar takes up to 30% of the horizontal space, and the remaining 10% is whitespace and padding. Treat it as a guideline, not a hard law - nudging the percentages to fit a design is expected.
ptrs: 60% dominant: sets the overall tone; typically the background; keep it neutral or low-saturation so everything else can breathe.
30% secondary: complements the dominant color on smaller areas - sidebars, cards, secondary sections - adding contrast and interest.
10% accent: the most vibrant color, spent only on call-to-action buttons and the few elements that must be noticed.
Why it works: the shares guide the eye and build hierarchy - the interface feels organized before a single word is read.
Neobrutalist twist: the raw style's heavy black borders around components act as the 10% accent against a dominant backdrop.
Neumorphic twist: soft neutral background (60%), panels and cards (30%), tiny interactive elements plus subtle shadows and highlights (10%).
Grid echo: main content takes the big central share, a sidebar up to 30% of the width, and about 10% goes to whitespace and padding.
It is a guideline, not a law - adjust the percentages when the design asks for it.
items.why: You already arrange colors on every thumbnail and layout you touch - this gives the instinct a name and a ratio, bro. Next time a design feels noisy or flat, count the shares: usually the accent is eating 40% of the screen or the secondary is missing entirely.
items.example: A neobrutalist card UI from the article: dominant flat backdrop, high-contrast cards as the 30%, and the thick black outlines plus one loud button doing the 10% accent work - you can literally point at which pixels belong to which share.

questions.q: Which color should be the 60%?
questions.a: A neutral or low-saturation color that can carry large areas without overpowering the design - it usually covers the background.

questions.q: Where does the 10% accent go?
questions.a: On the elements that must be noticed first: call-to-action buttons and key interactive elements. Keeping it to 10% is what keeps it loud.

questions.q: Is the ratio mandatory?
questions.a: No - it is explicitly a guideline. Designers adjust the percentages to suit the design; the point is keeping a clear hierarchy of dominant, secondary and accent.

items.plain: Think of a thali plate: most of it is rice (the 60% backdrop), a good scoop of dal or sabzi sits beside it (the 30% supporting flavor), and then there is one tiny spoon of hot pickle (the 10% accent). The pickle is small on purpose - if half the plate were pickle, dinner would be chaos.
items.image_caption: Blocks to scale: dominant 60% - secondary 30% - accent 10%.

items.headline: The jump cut: breaking the spell on purpose
items.deck: Remove a few frames from the middle of one continuous shot and time visibly lurches forward - a 'mistake' Jean-Luc Godard turned into film grammar in Breathless (1960).
items.lead: A jump cut is an editing technique in which some frames are taken out of a sequence, so the subject appears to leap forward in time inside the same framing. The Columbia Film Language Glossary notes it is typically used to draw the audience's attention to the conventions of filmmaking itself - and its reference example is the lunch-date scene from Jean-Luc Godard's Breathless (1960).
items.body: A jump cut is an editing technique in which some frames are taken out of a sequence, so the subject appears to leap forward in time inside the same framing. The Columbia Film Language Glossary notes it is typically used to draw the audience's attention to the conventions of filmmaking itself - and its reference example is the lunch-date scene from Jean-Luc Godard's Breathless (1960). Classical continuity editing works hard to hide the cut: matched eyelines, matched movement, steady framing, all so the story flows and the machinery stays invisible. The jump cut refuses the deal. The framing barely changes but time has skipped, and the viewer feels the splice - the edit announces that you are watching a constructed film, which is exactly why the glossary says it points at the conventions of the medium. Once you know the mechanic, you spot it everywhere: any time a creator trims a pause out of a single talking-head take and the head snaps slightly on screen, that is the same device, just used to compress time rather than provoke. The same removal of frames, two very different intentions.
ptrs: Definition (Columbia Film Language Glossary): an editing technique in which some frames are taken out of a sequence.
The effect: framing stays nearly the same but time visibly jumps, so the viewer feels the splice instead of gliding past it.
The point: it is typically used to draw attention to the conventions of filmmaking - the cut deliberately shows the machinery.
Canonical example: the lunch-date scene in Breathless (1960), directed by Jean-Luc Godard - the glossary's reference clip for the term.
Why it was radical: classical continuity editing exists to make cuts invisible; the jump cut flaunts the cut instead.
Where you see it daily: trimming dead air from one static talking-head take produces a jump cut - same frame removal, smaller ambitions.
items.why: This is the cheapest film-grammar lesson there is, bro: one snip, instantly visible. After today you will catch jump cuts in every vlog and every interview, and you will know the same trick that trims your reels is the one that once scandalized cinema.
items.example: Try the glossary's Breathless lunch-date clip first. Then make your own: film a static shot of your desk for 30 seconds, cut five seconds out of the middle, and watch your mug teleport. That lurch is the whole lesson.

questions.q: What exactly is removed in a jump cut?
questions.a: Frames from the middle of one continuous sequence. The framing stays nearly identical, so the removed time reads as a visible 'jump'.

questions.q: Why would a director want the cut to be visible?
questions.a: Per the Columbia glossary, it draws the audience's attention to the conventions of filmmaking itself - a deliberate break from editing designed to be invisible.

questions.q: Which film made it famous?
questions.a: The glossary's reference example is Breathless (1960) by Jean-Luc Godard, specifically the lunch-date scene.

items.plain: Record yourself saying one long sentence, delete the middle two seconds, and play it back. Your face snaps forward like it teleported. That little snap is a jump cut - and Godard built a classic on it in 1960.
items.image_alt: A paper filmstrip with two middle frames torn out, and a small clock whose hand has jumped forward.
items.info_alt: Diagram of a five-frame filmstrip: frames kept at both ends, two middle frames ghosted with torn edges, an arrow skipping over them.
items.info_caption: Keep - remove - keep: the frames come out of the middle of one unbroken shot, and time lurches.

items.headline: Anthropic's new flagship wears two name tags
items.deck: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are the same underlying model - Fable ships to everyone with cyber and bio safeguards, Mythos through verification programs. It posts the top coding score of any released model, and third-party tests crown it smartest, slowest and priciest at once.
items.lead: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2: the same underlying model under two names, where Fable carries cyber and bio safeguards and is broadly available, while Mythos is served through Anthropic's verification programs. Fable 5.2 scores 49.1% on FrontierCode 2.0 at Xhigh effort - the highest of any released model Anthropic tested - and tops the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 65, ranked #1 of 74, while also being flagged by Artificial Analysis as expensive, slow per task and very verbose.
items.body: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2: the same underlying model under two names, where Fable carries cyber and bio safeguards and is broadly available, while Mythos is served through Anthropic's verification programs. Fable 5.2 scores 49.1% on FrontierCode 2.0 at Xhigh effort - the highest of any released model Anthropic tested - and tops the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 65, ranked #1 of 74, while also being flagged by Artificial Analysis as expensive, slow per task and very verbose. FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether a model's code changes would be merged by the maintainers of open-source repositories; comparison best scores: Opus 5.5 at 45.5%, GPT-6 Astra at 42.8%, Gemini 4 Carbon at 41.1% (Medium effort), and Fable 5.1 at 32.4%. Anthropic also notes Fable 5.2 at High effort roughly matches Opus 5.5's Max-effort score (45.3% vs 45.5%) for about half the cost per task. Pricing is $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output, with an optional fast mode up to 2.5x faster at $16/$80; output runs up to 30% faster than Fable 5.1 at equal settings. Artificial Analysis' independent run agrees on the crown (65, #1 of 74) but adds the fine print: $26.54 per benchmark task, 46.4 minutes per task against a 12.7-minute median, and 275 million output tokens against a 72.8M median - the smartest reasoning run they measured is also a marathon. Anthropic's own usage advice matches: keep Opus 5.5 as the daily driver and reach for Fable or Mythos as an Advisor on the hardest steps or an Orchestrator coordinating cheaper models. The stunts are real too: an engineer had Fable 5.2 design a prototype operating system from an empty folder - over 1,000 subagents worked for eight days and produced a booting OS; a 1,000-agent team formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours where an earlier research Claude needed 11 days; and it solved two open problems in black-hole physics, described in linked preprints.
ptrs: Two names, one model: Fable 5.2 = Mythos 5.2 underneath. Fable carries cyber/bio safeguards and is available to everyone; Mythos runs through Anthropic's verification programs (its cybersecurity skills via the Cyber Verification Program).
Coding crown: 49.1% on FrontierCode 2.0 at Xhigh effort - the highest of any released model tested. The benchmark asks whether real open-source maintainers would merge the model's changes.

Field context: Opus 5.5 45.5%, GPT-6 Astra 42.8%, Gemini 4 Carbon 41.1% (Medium effort), Fable 5.1 32.4% - and Fable at High effort matches Opus 5.5's best (45.3% vs 45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task.

Third-party check: Artificial Analysis scores it 65 on its Intelligence Index, #1 of 74 - and simultaneously flags it as expensive, slow (46.4 min per task vs a 12.7 median) and very verbose (275M output tokens vs 72.8M median).
Price: $8 per million input tokens, $40 per million output; fast mode up to 2.5x speed at $16/$80; output is up to 30% faster than Fable 5.1.
Stunt of the week: from an empty folder, Fable 5.2 coordinated 1,000+ subagents for eight days and produced a working, bootable prototype operating system.

More receipts: 1,000 Fable agents formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours (an earlier research Claude took 11 days), and the model solved two open black-hole physics problems (preprints linked by Anthropic).
Anthropic's own advice: Opus 5.5 stays the daily driver; use Fable/Mythos as Advisor for the hardest steps or Orchestrator over cheaper models.
items.why: Notice the pattern, bro: the 'best' model is not the default tool, it is the specialist you call in. Opus for the daily grind, Fable as the advisor over the top - that orchestrator layout is the same cheap-model-first idea you keep meeting, just at the frontier end.
items.example: The OS stunt: one engineer, one empty folder, and Fable 5.2 spinning up over a thousand subagents that wrote, tested and reviewed code around the clock for eight days - ending in an operating system that actually boots, with drivers, windows, a login screen and an installer.

questions.q: What is the difference between Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2?
questions.a: They are the same underlying model. Fable ships with cyber and bio safeguards and is broadly available; Mythos is served through Anthropic's verification programs for restricted-capability work.

questions.q: What does FrontierCode 2.0 measure?
questions.a: Whether a model's code changes would be merged by the maintainers of open-source repositories - a real-engineering test, not a quiz.

questions.q: Is it the model to use every day?
questions.a: Anthropic says no: Opus 5.5 is the recommended daily driver, with Fable/Mythos used as an Advisor on the hardest steps or an Orchestrator coordinating cheaper models. Artificial Analysis also flags its cost, speed and verbosity.

items.plain: Same engine, two license plates: Fable is the version anyone can drive, Mythos needs a special permit. It just set the lap record for coding - but it drives slow, drinks fuel like a truck, and even its makers say keep your regular car for daily errands.

items.headline: Google's new fine print: humans may review what Gemini sees
items.deck: Google's own help page for Gemini's Connected Apps now says your Gmail, Drive and Photos data is 'used and human reviewed' - and flatly warns you not to connect apps holding confidential info. A user's tests show files can slide into chats without being @-tagged.
items.lead: Google's official 'About personalization with Connected Apps' help page confirms that when you connect Workspace apps like Gmail, Drive and Calendar to Gemini, that data is 'used and human reviewed per the Gemini Apps Privacy Notice,' and warns: 'Please don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see.' Separately, GitHub user thisisme6598 published tests showing connected files and emails can be pulled into casual chats even without @Drive or @Gmail tags - sometimes verbatim.
items.body: Google's official 'About personalization with Connected Apps' help page confirms that when you connect Workspace apps like Gmail, Drive and Calendar to Gemini, that data is 'used and human reviewed per the Gemini Apps Privacy Notice,' and warns: 'Please don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see.' Separately, GitHub user thisisme6598 published tests showing connected files and emails can be pulled into casual chats even without @Drive or @Gmail tags - sometimes verbatim. What Google's page says directly: a subset of Connected Apps data processed by Gemini is reviewed by human reviewers, 'including trained service providers,' to debug, keep services safe and improve them; Google says interactions are disconnected from your account and personal information is reduced before review, except for abuse or harm cases. On training, Google says it does not train generative models directly on your Gmail inbox, Drive, or Photos library - but it does train on summaries, excerpts and inferences from your emails and files, adding that 'in some cases... the summary may just be the email or file.' The community layer comes from thisisme6598's GitHub repo, which is attribution rather than independent confirmation: they document that Gemini Workspace extensions launched in 2023 promising personal content 'is not seen by human reviewers,' and argue the updated help answer plus an October 16 edit to that 2023 post quietly reversed it. In their testing, casually mentioning a personal topic (no tags) sometimes triggered background Workspace lookups with four possible outcomes - nothing pulled, a metadata-level summary, an exact quote containing names or account numbers, or a full file dump. Because the behavior is nondeterministic, a single clean test does not disprove it. The repo's own example: asking 'I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service' variously returned a generic answer, a bill summary, the full name-account-confirmation block from an email, or the entire email including headers. What you can actually do: manage or disconnect apps under Personal Intelligence settings, delete Gemini Apps activity, and turn off Keep Activity to stop future chats from being used to improve Google AI - with the caveat that deleting activity does not pull back data already reviewed.
ptrs: Google's help page, in its own words: Connected Apps data is 'used and human reviewed per the Gemini Apps Privacy Notice.'
The blunt warning, also verbatim: 'Please don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see.'
Training nuance: no direct training on your raw inbox, Drive or Photos - but summaries, excerpts and inferences ARE used, and 'in some cases... the summary may just be the email or file.'

Human review scope: a subset of processed Connected Apps data goes to human reviewers including trained service providers; Google says it disconnects interactions from your account and reduces personal info first, except for abuse or harm.

The reversal claim is attribution: GitHub user thisisme6598 documents the 2023 launch promise ('not seen by human reviewers') and the October 16 edit to that post - treat the 'quiet reversal' framing as theirs.

Their tests (also attribution): ambient mentions of personal topics sometimes pulled Drive/Gmail content with no @-tags, landing in one of four states - nothing, a metadata summary, an exact PII-laden quote, or a full file dump.
Nondeterministic by design: the ingestion is probabilistic, so one clean run proves nothing - the repo says delete the conversation and try again.
Your moves: disconnect apps in Personal Intelligence, delete Gemini Apps activity, turn off Keep Activity; note that already-reviewed data stays reviewed.
items.why: You live inside Gmail and Drive, bro, so this one is homework, not news: check whether Connected Apps are on in your Gemini settings and decide on purpose. Bigger lesson for the AIML shelf too - vendor privacy promises are versioned documents, not laws, and the changelog is the story.
items.example: The repo author's own test: with Connected Apps on, they asked Gemini 'I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service.' Across separate fresh chats it answered with (1) a generic guess, (2) 'Gmail search shows a bill of $122 on September 4', (3) an exact quote containing the full name, account number and confirmation number, and (4) the entire email dump including headers.

questions.q: Does Google say humans review my connected Gmail or Drive content?
questions.a: Yes - its help page states a subset of Connected Apps data processed by Gemini is reviewed by human reviewers, including trained service providers, and warns against connecting apps with confidential information.

questions.q: Does Google train models on my inbox?
questions.a: It says models are not trained directly on your Gmail inbox, Drive or Photos library, but are trained on summaries, excerpts and inferences from them - and notes the summary 'may just be the email or file.'

questions.q: How do I turn this off?
questions.a: Manage or disconnect apps under Personal Intelligence settings, delete Gemini Apps activity, and switch off Keep Activity to stop future chats being used to improve Google AI. Already-reviewed data is not pulled back.

items.headline: Fold a world-record paper plane tonight
items.deck: Foldable Flight catalogs 109 paper airplanes with step-by-step guides, difficulty levels, and speed and glide scores - its creator's Firefly 5 prototype can fly over 300 feet. One A4 sheet is all you need.
items.lead: Foldable Flight is a free library of 109 paper airplane designs, each with step-by-step folding instructions, a difficulty level, and separate Speed and Glide scores out of 10. Its headline design, Firefly 5, is a world-record prototype the site says can fly over 300 feet - and every plane in the catalog starts from one ordinary sheet of paper.
items.body: Foldable Flight is a free library of 109 paper airplane designs, each with step-by-step folding instructions, a difficulty level, and separate Speed and Glide scores out of 10. Its headline design, Firefly 5, is a world-record prototype the site says can fly over 300 feet - and every plane in the catalog starts from one ordinary sheet of paper. The catalog is built for browsing by feel: filter the planes, read the ratings, and pick something beginner-level for a first build. The speed-versus-glide split is the quiet lesson here - the site scores them as two different properties, which means every fold is a small tradeoff you are tuning, not just a shape you are copying. The drill: fold one simple dart, then throw it five times from the same spot with the same smooth motion and note the best distance. Now sharpen every crease with a fingernail or the back of a spoon, check that the wings are symmetrical (the wingtips should line up when folded flat), and throw five more. Change exactly one thing per round and keep count - that is a real experiment loop with n=5, run at your desk for zero rupees.
ptrs: The site: Foldable Flight, a free catalog of 109 paper airplane designs with step-by-step folding instructions for each.
Every plane carries a difficulty level plus separate Speed and Glide scores out of 10 - two different properties, so each design is a tradeoff you can tune.
The flex: the site's Firefly 5 is a world-record prototype it says can fly over 300 feet.
Tonight's drill: fold one simple beginner dart, throw it five times from the same spot, and write down the best distance.
Then iterate: sharpen every crease, line up the wingtips for symmetry, and throw five more - changing exactly one thing per round.
Why five throws: one lucky throw lies; a best-of-five starts to look like measurement. You are running a tiny experiment, not just playing.
items.why: Zero setup, zero screen, and it sneaks in the exact skill that transfers to everything else you build, bro: change one variable, measure, repeat. Also, a 300-foot paper plane is the kind of bar bet worth having in your pocket.
items.example: Fold your first dart in five minutes, mark a launch spot on the floor with tape, and run two rounds of five throws - sloppy folds versus sharpened, symmetrical folds. The distance gap between the two rounds is your craftsmanship made visible.

questions.q: Where do I start?
questions.a: Pick any beginner-level design on Foldable Flight - each comes with step-by-step instructions and shows its Speed and Glide scores before you fold.

questions.q: What do the Speed and Glide scores mean?
questions.a: They are the site's per-plane ratings out of 10 for two separate flight properties - how fast a design flies versus how long it stays aloft - so you can pick for distance or for float.

questions.q: How do I make my plane fly farther?
questions.a: The drill in this issue: sharp creases, symmetrical wings (wingtips aligned), one change at a time, and best-of-five throws from the same spot so you can actually see the effect.

items.plain: This is the cheapest engineering lab on Earth: one sheet of paper. Fold, throw five times, sharpen the creases, throw again, and watch the numbers move. Same loop as training a model - data, tweak, measure - except the loss function is your living-room floor.

items.headline: Your RAM is the GPU you forgot
items.deck: A new open-source project runs a 284-billion-parameter model on a plain 64GB CPU box - no GPU at all - and 30B models on ordinary 16-32GB machines. The trick is savage quantization plus CPU-cache wizardry. One of its models fits your rig TODAY.
items.lead: llama-modchip, a brand-new open-source project (Apache 2.0), patches llama.cpp to run sparse Mixture-of-Experts models entirely in system RAM: its headline act squeezes DeepSeek-V4-Flash's 284.33B parameters (only 13.17B active per token) into a 56.56 GiB file that runs on a 64GB CPU-only machine at 9.1-14.7 tokens/second. More relevant to you: its 30B model tier targets ordinary 16-32GB machines, and its 8B model fits comfortably today.
items.body: llama-modchip, a brand-new open-source project (Apache 2.0), patches llama.cpp to run sparse Mixture-of-Experts models entirely in system RAM: its headline act squeezes DeepSeek-V4-Flash's 284.33B parameters (only 13.17B active per token) into a 56.56 GiB file that runs on a 64GB CPU-only machine at 9.1-14.7 tokens/second. More relevant to you: its 30B model tier targets ordinary 16-32GB machines, and its 8B model fits comfortably today. The recipe has three parts. First, brutal but careful quantization: the 284B checkpoint is compressed to 1.71 bits per weight on average (routed experts at 1.5625 bpw, sensitive layers kept higher), shrinking it from 76.87 GiB to 56.56 GiB so model plus a 256K-token context lock into 64GB of RAM with zero swap. Second, CPU kernel patches that tile the math across registers and L1/L2/L3 caches, lifting prompt processing on a 16-core Zen 5 from 25.0 to 44.36 tok/s (+77%). Third, a tiny 1.64 MB n-gram 'drafter' (borrowed from chess-engine thinking) that guesses tokens ahead for the big model to verify, plus 13-32 millisecond snapshots that restore a whole agent session's memory near-instantly. The model menu by hardware: Nemotron-H-8B (dense, 4.60-8.00 GiB) fits your current 16GB RAM easily, and its 4.6 GiB Q4 file is smaller than your 6GB of VRAM - though the project's verified all-GPU setups are 8-11GB cards. The 30B MoEs (Nemotron-3.5-30B, Qwen3-30B at 14.35-17.6 GiB) are classed for 16-32GB machines: on your current 16GB with Windows running that's the razor's edge, and on the 32GB you're considering it becomes comfortable - author-reported speeds are 25.0-60.4 tok/s on a 16-core Ryzen 9 9955HX. The 284B needs 64GB, beyond even your planned upgrade. There's a Windows 10/11 pack that auto-detects cores, RAM and VRAM and splits the model between GPU and CPU RAM. Caveats: the custom Fractal-64 quantization uses a tensor type stock llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio refuse, so you must use the project's own binary; it's a one-month-old, mostly single-author repo, so treat its benchmarks as author-reported; and your CPU is unknown, so expect slower than the Zen 5 numbers.
ptrs: The headline trick: DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284.33B params, 13.17B active) quantized to 56.56 GiB (1.71 bits/weight avg) runs on 64GB CPU-only at 9.1-14.7 tok/s decode, 43-44 tok/s prefill - zero GPUs, zero swap, 256K context.

How: aggressive quantization (routed experts at 1.5625 bpw, sensitive layers preserved higher), 4-level register/L1/L2/L3 cache-tiled CPU kernels (+77% prefill), a 1.64 MB speculative 'drafter', and 13-32ms session restore snapshots.
What fits YOUR rig today: Nemotron-H-8B at 4.60-8.00 GiB slides into 16GB RAM easily; the 4.6 GiB Q4 file is under your 6GB VRAM, though the project's verified all-GPU setups are 8-11GB cards.
The 30B MoEs (14.35-17.6 GiB) are the 16-32GB tier: razor's edge on your current 16GB Windows setup, comfortable on the 32GB you're considering. The 284B needs 64GB - beyond the planned upgrade.
Windows is supported: a Windows 10/11 pack detects cores, RAM and VRAM and splits the model across GPU and CPU RAM automatically.

Caveats: Fractal-64 files use a custom tensor type that stock llama.cpp/Ollama/LM Studio reject (use the project's binary); the repo is one month old and mostly single-author, so benchmarks are author-reported; speeds quoted are from a 16-core Zen 5 and yours will vary. HN discussion: ~365 points.
items.why: Bro, everyone told you local AI needs a fat GPU. This project says the RAM you already have is the real playground - an 8B model runs on your machine tonight, free, no API bill, no queue. And if you do bump to 32GB, a whole 30B tier unlocks. That's not an upgrade, that's an unlockable character.
items.example: Concrete tonight experiment: grab the Nemotron-H-8B build (4.6 GiB), run the project's Windows pack, and you have a private chat model answering from your own machine - the same file size as two phone photos per parameter-short model, zero API key.

questions.q: How does a 284B model fit in 64GB of RAM?
questions.a: Two tricks: only 13.17B of its parameters are active per token (Mixture-of-Experts), and the whole checkpoint is quantized to about 1.71 bits per weight - a 56.56 GiB file that locks into RAM with zero swap.

questions.q: Which tier fits Rudy's current 16GB RAM and 6GB VRAM?
questions.a: The 8B dense model (4.60-8.00 GiB) fits easily in RAM; the 30B tier is the razor's edge on 16GB and comfortable on 32GB; the 284B needs 64GB.

questions.q: Why can't you just load these files in Ollama?
questions.a: The custom Fractal-64 quantization uses a tensor type (Q2_0, ID 40) that stock llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio reject - you need the project's own patched binary.

items.plain: Big AI models are like libraries: you don't need every book open at once, just the right shelf. These models keep most 'books' compressed tiny and only pull out the shelf needed for each word. That's why a huge model can live in ordinary computer memory instead of an expensive graphics card.

items.headline: Measure twice, cut once, render first
items.deck: KetchUp is a free, open-source 3D modeling app for furniture and woodworking - draw a rectangle, pull it into a board, orbit around your table before you buy a single plank. Runs in your browser or as a Windows app, no account, MIT license.
items.lead: KetchUp is a free, open-source 3D modeling app (MIT license, written in Rust) for planning woodworking and furniture projects with exact measurements before you build. It runs in a desktop browser (WebGPU or WebGL2) or as a native Windows, macOS or Linux app - no account, no cloud, no subscription.
items.body: KetchUp is a free, open-source 3D modeling app (MIT license, written in Rust) for planning woodworking and furniture projects with exact measurements before you build. It runs in a desktop browser (WebGPU or WebGL2) or as a native Windows, macOS or Linux app - no account, no cloud, no subscription. The workflow is deliberately simple: draw lines, rectangles, circles or freehand outlines on the ground plane; use Push/Pull to turn faces into solid forms; then move, scale, offset and paint. Precision is the point: you snap to geometry and axes, type exact lengths, and check the result with Tape Measure and Dimensions tools. Bigger projects stay organized with groups, reusable components and tags, and you orbit around the assembly to review proportions before taking it to the workshop. Your work autosaves locally on your device, and File > Save downloads a portable .ketchup project you can keep (clearing browser data can erase autosaved work, so download what matters). It imports SketchUp (.skp) geometry - textures, scenes and some model features aren't supported - and exports Wavefront OBJ geometry without materials, so it slots into a bigger 3D pipeline. The name is a wink at SketchUp, and the HN crowd (~199 points) received it as an open-source SketchUp alternative; the tradeoffs are real too - it's early (v0.6.5), aimed at desktop with mouse and keyboard, and focused on furniture-scale work rather than everything SketchUp does. For a first project, the site's own starter is three steps: draw a rectangle, Push/Pull it into depth, then Orbit (press F to fit) and look at your creation from every side.
ptrs: What it is: free, open-source (MIT, Rust) 3D modeling for woodworking and furniture - shelves, tables, cabinets, workbenches - with exact measurements.
Where it runs: desktop browser with WebGPU/WebGL2, or native Windows, macOS and Linux apps; no account, no cloud; autosaves locally, download portable .ketchup files to keep.
Core workflow: draw rectangles/lines/circles, Push/Pull faces into solid forms, move/scale/offset/paint; snap to axes, type exact lengths, check with Tape Measure and Dimensions.
Organization: groups, reusable components, tags; orbit the assembly to check proportions before cutting anything.
Interop and limits: imports SketchUp .skp geometry (textures/scenes/some features unsupported), exports OBJ without materials; early version (v0.6.5), desktop + mouse focused.
HN received it (~199 points) as an open-source SketchUp alternative - the free price is real, the feature gap versus full SketchUp is too.
items.why: You keep designing in 2D, bro - flat layouts, flat thumbnails. This is your free ticket to thinking in 3D space, which shows up everywhere: game assets, product mockups, agency pitch visuals. Zero rupees, no signup, runs on your PC tonight.
items.example: The site's own starter project: draw one rectangle on the ground plane, choose Push/Pull and drag it into a solid block, then Orbit (press F to fit) - three steps from empty canvas to a 3D object you can inspect from every angle.

questions.q: What does KetchUp cost and what does it need to run?
questions.a: It's free and open source (MIT). It runs in a desktop browser with WebGPU/WebGL2 or as a native Windows/macOS/Linux app - no account needed.

questions.q: What is Push/Pull?
questions.a: KetchUp's core move: draw a flat face (like a rectangle), then pull it outward to give it thickness and turn it into a solid 3D form.

questions.q: Can it open SketchUp files?
questions.a: It imports .skp geometry, but textures, scenes and some model features aren't supported; it exports OBJ geometry without materials.

items.plain: Imagine drawing a square on paper, then grabbing its edge and pulling it up into a real cardboard box - that's the whole idea of 3D modeling here. You sketch flat shapes, stretch them into solid boards, and walk around your furniture on screen before spending money on wood.

items.headline: Tilt the camera, tilt the mood
items.deck: One small rotation - camera rolled off level - and a normal room feels wrong. The Dutch angle is cinema's cheapest unease machine, and its name is a 100-year-old translation mistake. Here's when it works and when it just looks like a tripod accident.
items.lead: The Dutch angle - also called Dutch tilt, canted or oblique angle - is a shot where the camera is rolled off its level axis so the whole frame sits off-kilter, making viewers feel like their heads are tilted. Filmmakers use it to pour unease, tension and disorientation into a scene without changing anything else.
items.body: The Dutch angle - also called Dutch tilt, canted or oblique angle - is a shot where the camera is rolled off its level axis so the whole frame sits off-kilter, making viewers feel like their heads are tilted. Filmmakers use it to pour unease, tension and disorientation into a scene without changing anything else. The name is a historical accident: Soviet filmmaker Dziga Vertov used the tilt famously in 1929's Man With a Movie Camera, and German Expressionist horror The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920) made it part of its twisted visual style - 'Deutsch' (German) got mistranslated into 'Dutch', and the wrong name stuck for a century. What it does to an audience: portrays uneasiness and tension, puts viewers on edge, builds a dark or ominous mood, and heightens emotion, especially in close-up - a character in peril or discovering something disturbing feels abstract, subjective, disoriented, all from slanting the camera a little. It's also a deliberate exception to Roger Deakins' rule that the best cinematography doesn't stand out but fits within the movie: the Dutch angle wants to push viewers out of their comfort zone. The craft rules: use it sparingly, because the shot loses weight in every extra scene; vary the degrees of tilt - a small cant reads as quietly uncanny, a steep one as full chaos; try different focal lengths (wide, medium, close) and don't be afraid to move the camera while tilted; test the frame, because tilting picks up background you didn't plan; and think about the shots before and after, since the tilt only lands if the edit makes it disruptive. Famous uses: 1966's Batman ran it as a visual pun - every villain's lair sat crooked; Sam Raimi sells Ash's chaos with it in Evil Dead II; Brian De Palma's Mission: Impossible (1996) steepens the tilts mid-conversation as things turn worse; Inception tilted a whole hallway fight; Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas weaponized it for drug sequences.
ptrs: Definition: camera rolled off its level axis - the frame sits canted and viewers feel like their own head is tilted; also called Dutch tilt, canted or oblique angle.
Effect: unease, tension, ominous mood, disorientation - strongest in close-up, when a character is in peril or discovering something disturbing.
Name origin: used famously by Dziga Vertov (Man With a Movie Camera, 1929) and German Expressionism (The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, 1920) - 'Deutsch' (German) was mistranslated as 'Dutch'.

Craft rules: use sparingly; vary tilt degrees (small = uncanny, steep = chaos); try wide/medium/close focal lengths; movement while tilted adds to it; test for surprise background; consider the shots before and after in the edit.

Canon examples: Batman (1966) tilted every villain lair as a visual pun; Evil Dead II sells chaos; Mission: Impossible (1996) steepens the tilt as a conversation turns; Inception's hallway fight; Fear and Loathing's drug scenes.
The Deakins tension: his rule says the best cinematography fits the movie without standing out - the Dutch angle is the sanctioned exception.
items.why: Bro, your reels cut fast but they all sit LEVEL. One 15-degree tilt on the frame where the tutorial goes wrong - 'the bug appears' - and your viewers FEEL it before you say a word. Free production value, zero plugins, just rotate the phone.
items.example: Mission: Impossible (1996): a conversation between Ethan Hunt and his handler starts with a mild tilt and the angle gets steeper as the news gets worse - the camera's lean IS the rising dread, no dialogue needed.

questions.q: What is a Dutch angle?
questions.a: A shot where the camera is rolled off its level axis so the frame sits off-kilter - used to create unease, tension and disorientation.

questions.q: Why is it called 'Dutch'?
questions.a: It's a mistranslation: the style came from German cinema ('Deutsch'), and 'Deutsch' was mistranslated as 'Dutch'.

questions.q: What's the main craft rule?
questions.a: Use it sparingly - the shot loses its weight if it appears in too many scenes, so save it for genuinely heightened moments.

items.plain: Hold your phone perfectly straight and film a doorway - it looks normal. Now tilt your hand sideways and film it again: same doorway, but suddenly it feels like something is wrong. Filmmakers use that tilt on purpose to make you nervous without any monsters at all.
items.info_caption: Diagram: level camera, level horizon - tilt the camera and every line in the frame leans with it.
